body: In Marlborough, a large share of the houses that need siding repair are rental buildings. Only about 56 percent of homes in the city are owner-occupied, and a two-family with a cracked corner, a loose run of vinyl or a rotted porch skirt is better fixed now than left for the next turnover. Small repairs done early keep water out of sheathing that, on older buildings, may be more than a century old.

A good repair starts with finding where the water came from. Rot at the bottom of a wall usually traces to splashback from a gutter that overflows or a downspout that dumps against the foundation. Damage around a porch often comes from a ledger board that was never flashed or a porch roof that sheds water against the siding. Wet patches below windows point to failed head or sill flashing. Fixing the siding without fixing the cause just schedules the same repair again.

Matching comes next. On prewar houses, measure the exposure and profile of the existing clapboard or shingles, because new stock may not be the same size. On vinyl or aluminum from the 1960s and 1970s, the original profile may be discontinued and the color faded, so taking panels from a less visible wall for the front repair is a common workaround. Houses built before 1978 call for lead-safe work practices when painted surfaces are disturbed beyond small areas. If repairs keep multiplying on a Marlborough building, it is worth pricing a partial or full re-side to compare.

faq.q: My Marlborough rental has rot under the porch. Is that a siding repair or a bigger problem?
faq.a: It can be either. Rot at the porch often starts where the ledger board meets the house without proper flashing, so water runs behind the siding and into the sheathing. A contractor should open the area to check how far the damage goes. If it is limited to siding and trim, a repair with new flashing will fix it. If the rim joist or ledger is soft, the porch attachment itself needs work.

body: A complete re-side on a Marlborough building is often a project on rental property, and that changes the planning. With roughly 17 percent of the city's housing in two- to four-unit buildings and only about 44 percent in single detached houses, many jobs involve tenants, stacked porches, shared driveways and tight side yards. Agree on a schedule, debris plan and parking arrangement before the first wall comes down.

On a prewar building, the tear-off may reveal board sheathing laid more than a hundred years ago, often with gaps, old nail holes and soft spots near the porches. Bad boards get replaced, and very uneven walls may get a layer of plywood or furring to give the new siding a flat base. Then comes a continuous weather barrier and new flashing at every window, door and porch ledger. On a postwar house, the sheathing is usually plywood or fiberboard, and the main checks are window corners and the sill plate. Either way, any painted layer on a building older than 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe requirements, which include protecting occupants.

The new material is a separate decision. Vinyl keeps costs down on large multi-family walls, fiber cement holds paint far longer than wood, and clapboard or shingles suit the older houses near Marlborough Center. Whatever you choose, decide on trim, soffits and porch details at the same time so they are installed together. Ask each bidder in Marlborough for a written scope, the order in which walls will be done, and how unexpected rot will be priced.

faq.q: What should a full siding contract include for a Marlborough two-family?
faq.a: It should describe removal and disposal of old siding, how lead paint will be handled if the house predates 1978, the weather barrier and flashing details, the new siding and trim, and how hidden rot will be priced. For rentals, add the work schedule, tenant notice, porch and stair access, and where debris and materials will be staged. A clear written scope prevents disputes later.

body: Marlborough's gutters have to cope with three different situations. Downtown, big gable roofs on multi-family buildings collect a lot of water in a small area and send it onto narrow lots and shared driveways. On the city's slopes, roof water wants to run downhill toward a foundation or a neighbor's yard. And around Lake Williams and the reservoirs, trees drop leaves and needles that clog a gutter in one season.

Size comes first. A large roof needs a gutter and downspouts big enough for a heavy summer cloudburst; a standard size can overflow at the corners of a three-decker. Count how much roof drains to each outlet and add downspouts where a single one has to carry a long run. Where the discharge goes matters just as much. Water should leave the downspout onto ground that slopes away from the foundation, and it should not end up across a shared driveway, where it freezes in winter, or on the lot next door.

Seamless aluminum, formed on site, works for most Marlborough houses and leaves only corners and outlets as seams. Hang it on hidden hangers fastened into solid fascia, and replace any rotted fascia board before the new gutter goes up. On wooded lots near the water, a guard reduces cleaning but still needs a look each fall. Winter ice at the eaves is usually a sign of heat loss from the attic, so if icicles form every year, ask about insulation and ventilation as well.

faq.q: Where should downspouts drain on a Marlborough multi-family with a shared driveway?
faq.a: Away from the foundation and off paved surfaces where possible. Water discharged across a shared driveway can freeze and become a hazard, and it may flow onto a neighbor's property. Options include extensions to a planted area that slopes away, buried pipe to a point lower on the lot, or a dry well where soil allows. Plan the outlets before the gutters are installed so the downspouts go where the drainage works.

body: Roofs in Marlborough come in two broad families. The nineteenth-century houses near Main Street and French Hill tend to have steep pitches, cross gables and dormers, with many valleys and wall joints to flash. The postwar ranches, split-levels and colonials built after the 1960s boom have simpler, lower-pitched roofs. A median build year of 1974 means many of the latter are now on their second roof at least.

Each family has its own problems. On older houses, the decking may still be wide boards with gaps between them, and those usually need a layer of plywood before modern shingles go on. Complex roofs also need new step flashing at each dormer wall, chimney counterflashing cut into mortar joints, and careful valley work. On low-slope postwar roofs, water moves slowly, so extra underlayment and a wider band of self-adhering membrane help keep wind-driven rain and meltwater out. On multi-family buildings, include porch roofs and dormers in the scope so the whole structure is covered.

At an elevation of about 450 feet, inland Marlborough sees snow that sits and freezes at the eaves, so an ice barrier along every eave and in every valley is standard. Ventilation matters as much as shingles: open soffit vents, a ridge vent and a sealed attic floor keep the deck cold and limit ice dams. Ask whether the bid includes a full tear-off to the deck, replacing damaged boards, and new drip edge. Architectural asphalt shingles nailed to the maker's pattern can serve twenty-five to fifty years on a well-ventilated roof.

faq.q: My Marlborough ranch has a low-pitch roof. Does that change how it should be reroofed?
faq.a: Yes. On a low-slope roof, water drains more slowly and wind can push it under shingles, so manufacturers call for extra underlayment, often a double layer or full self-adhering membrane, below a certain pitch. Very low slopes may be better suited to a membrane roof than shingles. Ask the contractor to measure the pitch and explain which underlayment the shingle maker requires for it.

body: When American Woolen auctioned its company houses in 1934, the south side of Maynard went from one landlord to dozens of individual owners almost overnight. Ninety years later, the Presidential district shows the result: houses built to the same plans now wear every kind of cladding, and vinyl is the most common of them. It is a practical match for these modest frame houses, and for the many ranches and capes that pushed the town's median build year to 1963.

What separates a good vinyl job here from a forgettable one is the openings. Company houses had simple but deliberate window and door casings, and when an installer buries them behind narrow J-channel, the house looks squinty next to its neighbors. Ask for wide flat casing or a lineal that keeps the original trim width. The old siding, often a mix of wood clapboard and a mid-century layer, should come off so sills and sheathing can be checked; on houses of this age, the removal must follow EPA lead-safe practice, with ground cover, containment and cleanup.

Hang the panels so they float. Every nail sits in the center of its slot with a little play, and each panel end stops short of the channel by the amount the maker specifies for the season of installation, since inland Middlesex winters and July heat move vinyl a surprising distance. Roughly one Maynard home in eight is in a two- to four-unit building, and on a two-family, doing both halves at once avoids a seam down the middle. Ask bidders about panel gauge, starter strip, and how outside corners will be trimmed.

faq.q: My house on Grant Street in Maynard looks like its neighbors. Should my vinyl match theirs?
faq.a: You are not required to match, but it helps to think about the row. The Presidential district houses were built as a set, and keeping a similar lap width and trim depth keeps your house in step with the street even if the color differs. The bigger choices are panel thickness, trim around the windows and whether the old layers come off. A careful tear-off and properly sized casings matter more to the result than the exact color.

body: Roughly a third of Maynard's housing predates 1940, and much of that older stock still has wood lap boards on the frame, sometimes buried under aluminum or vinyl from a later decade. In the old company neighborhood on the south side, streets like Grant, McKinley and Garfield are lined with houses built to a handful of designs, so a board with the wrong reveal on one house shows up right away against the one next door.

Before ordering stock, open up a sound patch of wall and record three numbers: how much of each course shows, how thick the butt edge is, and how wide the casings and corners run. Today's bevel stock often lands close without landing exactly, and when it misses, a local mill can knife a profile to suit. Coat each board with primer on the back and edges as well as the face, and seal ends where they butt into trim. Choose stainless fasteners so no rust streaks appear later. Furring the boards off the wrap by a small air space lets the wood shed moisture between storms, and paint on shaded walls holds up much longer as a result.

Lead is the other part of any clapboard job here. Paint on these houses goes back many decades, and with about 69 percent of the town built before 1980, scraping or removing it is regulated work under the EPA renovation rules. Converted churches on Summer, Walnut and Glendale streets have tall, wide walls of lap siding that need staging rather than ladders. On a two-family, plan the paint and board work for both units together.

faq.q: I found old clapboard under the aluminum on my Maynard house. Is it worth saving?
faq.a: Sometimes. Pull a few pieces of aluminum and look at the wood: if most boards are sound and only the lower courses or areas below windows are soft, the clapboard can be repaired, scraped under lead-safe rules, primed and painted. If the wood is split throughout or the nail holes from the aluminum have let water in, new clapboard over a fresh weather barrier is usually the better investment.

body: Fiber cement suits Maynard owners who want their early twentieth-century house to look painted and wooden again without the scrape-and-paint routine every several years. It reads much like original clapboard from the sidewalk, holds factory paint for a long time and does not rot. For a town where three in four homes are owner-occupied, the long service life is a reasonable trade for the extra work at installation.

That extra work shows up first on tight lots. On the south-side streets the company laid out, one house can stand a driveway's width from the next. Planks arrive in long, weighty bundles, and every saw cut lofts respirable silica, so before day one the crew should know where the stack will sit, where cutting happens, and how dust is kept off a neighbor's car and open windows. Electric shears or a vacuum-hooded blade belong on this job, and the written estimate should say how the yard will be protected.

On the wall, this product forgives very little. Plank ends that meet a porch or shed roof stay up off the shingles, with metal steps beneath and a diverter at the low end. The first course stays well up from dirt and walks, especially on low Assabet-side lots where splash and damp hang around. Paint every sawn edge and slip a small metal backer behind each spot where two planks meet end to end. On a two-family, re-cladding both sides together avoids a line down the middle and keeps the flashing continuous across the building.

faq.q: Is fiber cement heavy enough to cause problems on an older Maynard house?
faq.a: It is heavier than vinyl or wood, but a typical wood-frame house handles it without trouble. The concern is more about installation: boards must be fastened to framing or solid sheathing as the manufacturer specifies, and older walls with soft or gapped board sheathing may need repairs first. A tear-off shows the condition of the wall so those fixes can be made before the new siding goes on.

body: Cedar shingles in Maynard most often appear on the gables, porch walls and dormers of early twentieth-century houses, and on the old churches on Summer, Walnut and Glendale streets that have become homes. On a converted church, shingles can break up a tall, plain wall in a way lap siding cannot, and on a gable they add texture above the clapboard below.

The river shapes how shingles should be installed here. The Assabet runs through the middle of town, and houses on low ground near its banks sit in damp air for long stretches, especially in spring. Shingles have to dry from both faces, so a crinkled wrap or thin battens should hold them off the house. Start the first course a hand's width or more up from the soil, fasten with stainless, and leave a hairline space at each side joint to give the cedar room as it takes on humidity. Shingles set tight in a damp spot will cup and split within a few seasons.

Decide on a finish before the first course goes up. Bleaching oil lets cedar turn an even silver-gray over time; a semi-transparent stain adds color while showing grain; a solid stain hides variation but needs periodic renewal and can trap moisture if applied too thick. On a church or tall gable, plan for staging, since shingle work goes slowly and needs steady footing. If the old wall carries paint from before 1978, follow lead-safe practice when stripping it. Installed with good drying, cedar can last twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Can cedar shingles work on a Maynard house near the Assabet River?
faq.a: Yes, as long as they are installed to dry. Damp air near the river means shingles need a ventilated backing so moisture behind them can escape, plus stainless nails that will not corrode. Keep the bottom course well above the ground and clear of mulch. Shaded walls may grow mildew, so a finish with mildewcide or a regular wash helps. Done this way, shingles hold up well even on low lots.

body: On Maynard's mill-era houses, trim tends to fail before the siding does. Porch columns, window caps, sills and cornice returns have been painted so many times that the paint film hides how soft the wood underneath has become. The usual tell is a column base that crumbles under a screwdriver, or a sill that dips in the middle where water has been sitting for years.

The houses American Woolen built in 1902 and 1903, and the fifty that followed in 1918, share details from street to street. Replacing a rotted window cap or porch rail with a stock lumberyard profile makes one house stand out from its row. A better approach is to take the damaged piece, or a sound twin from another window, and have it copied. Where only the bottom of a casing or column is gone, a dutchman repair, cutting out the bad section and gluing in new wood, keeps the rest of the original.

Material choice should follow exposure. Cellular PVC is a smart fit for porch column bases, sill nosings and the lowest pieces of door casing, which sit in splash and snow; it needs glued joints and allowance for heat movement. Higher pieces with molded edges are often better in primed wood sealed on all sides. On converted churches, tall window surrounds and steep rakes call for staging and sometimes custom millwork. With the median Maynard home built in 1963 and many far older, scraping or removing painted trim usually triggers EPA lead-safe procedures.

faq.q: Do soft column bases on my Maynard porch mean the whole column has to go?
faq.a: Not necessarily. When decay stays in the bottom few inches, a carpenter can jack the porch roof slightly, saw off the bad end, and fit a new plinth or a glued-in splice, often PVC since that spot stays wet. If probing shows the rot climbing up the inside of a hollow column, a new column is the better buy. Either way, check that the porch floor drains away from the base so the repair does not repeat.

body: Plenty of Maynard siding problems are smaller than they first look. A few vinyl panels cracked by a snowblower, a corner board gone punky at the bottom, or shingles knocked loose on a gable can be handled as a repair. The question is whether the wall behind is sound and whether the damaged material can be matched closely enough to blend in.

On older houses, cutting into one layer often reveals another. Many homes from before 1940 have vinyl or aluminum over the original wood, sometimes with asphalt or asbestos-cement siding in between. Knowing what is under there before a repair begins avoids surprises, and any suspected asbestos layer should be tested before it is cut. Lead paint on the old wood means lead-safe practice once the disturbed area goes beyond a small patch.

A repair also has to stop the water that caused the damage. Corner boards rot when a gutter overflows above them or a downspout dumps at their base. Siding below a window fails when the sill slopes inward or the head has no drip cap. On low lots near the Assabet, ground moisture keeps the bottom courses damp, so raising the clearance between soil and siding may be part of the fix. On a two-family, the repaired side should match the other unit as closely as possible, and both owners should know what is being done. A written estimate that names the cause, the repair and any recommended follow-up keeps everyone clear.

faq.q: Will a siding repair on one half of my Maynard two-family stand out from the other half?
faq.a: It can if the materials differ, so matching matters. A contractor should identify the existing profile and color and look for a close current product, or take panels from a hidden spot on the building for the visible repair. Wood clapboard can be milled to match. If the two halves already differ in color from fading, talk with the other owner about whether repainting or re-siding one full wall makes more sense.

body: A full re-side in Maynard frequently means peeling back several generations at once. A house from 1903 might carry its original clapboard, a mid-century coat of tar-paper brick or cement-board shingles, and then a top coat of aluminum or vinyl. Each layer was nailed through the one before it, and moisture trapped between them can rot sheathing and sills that no one has seen in decades.

Send a chip of any cement-board shingle to a lab before demolition starts, because many contain asbestos, and set up lead-safe containment for the painted boards underneath. Once the frame is bare, rotten planks of board sheathing get swapped, crumbling sill timbers get sistered or replaced, and a fresh wrap goes on in shingle fashion. Every opening then gets a formed pan below and sealed laps on the sides and head. On low Assabet-side lots, the base of the wall deserves the most care, with a solid sill and enough height between the first course and the soil. Owners curious about foam board should raise it now, since it pushes every casing outward.

Two-family houses are common here, and replacing siding on both halves at once avoids a seam down the center of the building. That can mean two owners, or an owner and tenants, so schedule, access and colors should be agreed in writing before work starts. Ask contractors how they protect the house next door on tight lots, how they price hidden rot, and what weather barrier they use. The new material, vinyl, fiber cement, clapboard or shingle, is a separate choice once the wall itself is right.

faq.q: Should all the old layers come off when I re-side my Maynard house?
faq.a: Yes. Taking the wall down to bare boards is the only honest starting point, since every buried layer conceals rot and makes it harder to fit trim and metal correctly. If one layer is asbestos-cement shingle, it has to be tested and removed under state and federal rules, often by a licensed abatement contractor. Once the wall is bare, rot can be repaired and the new siding installed over a proper weather barrier and flashing.

body: Water in Maynard heads toward the Assabet. The land drops about 30 feet from the Stow line to the Acton line, and a large share of the town drains to the river that runs through its center. For houses on the lower streets near the banks, getting roof runoff away from the foundation is the main job a gutter system does, and the river's March 2010 flood is a reminder of how wet that ground can get.

Start with discharge. Each downspout should end well away from the house, either with an extension, a splash block on soil that slopes away, or a buried solid pipe carrying water to an outlet. On closely spaced houses, check where that water goes: dumping it toward a side yard can put it in the neighbor's basement instead of yours. Seamless aluminum in a 5- or 6-inch size suits most Maynard houses, with downspouts sized to the roof area each one serves.

Two-family houses with long shared eaves need extra thought. A single long run may need outlets at both ends or a center drop to avoid overflow during heavy rain, and both owners should agree on where downspouts land. Older houses with shallow or decorative eaves may need careful hanger placement so the gutter sits under the drip edge without covering trim. With about 44 inches of snow in an average winter, gutters can fill with ice; good attic insulation and ventilation reduce the meltwater that feeds those ice dams.

faq.q: My Maynard basement gets damp after storms. Can gutters fix that?
faq.a: Often they help a great deal. The key is moving roof water well past the foundation with extensions or buried pipe, and making sure the soil slopes away on every side. On low ground near the Assabet, groundwater can also play a part, and gutters alone will not solve that. If dampness continues after the gutters and grading are fixed, have a waterproofing specialist look at the foundation and drainage.

body: Maynard averages about 44 inches of snow a year, and many of its roofs sit on houses built in the early twentieth century, so a reroof here usually begins with a close look at what is underneath. Company houses from 1902 and 1903 often have plank decking, sometimes with two or more old shingle layers on top. Chimneys on those houses have often been patched with tar or caulk rather than properly reflashed.

Strip every layer down to the boards. Until the old shingles are off, nobody can see which planks are cracked, rotted at the eave or sagging between rafters, and each of those gets replaced. Plank decks with wide gaps or cupped boards are commonly covered with plywood so the new underlayment has an even surface. Chimneys on these houses deserve fresh step pieces plus counterflashing let into the mortar joints, and a wide one benefits from a small saddle on its uphill side. Dormer cheeks and sidewalls need the same new step work, with a kick-out at the bottom of each run, because the joints wear out decades before the shingles do.

Two-family houses add a wrinkle. Many have long rooflines shared between units, and both owners need to agree to a single project so flashing and underlayment run unbroken across the building. Self-adhering ice barrier should cover each eave and valley, reaching upslope past where the wall below sits. Airflow has to work along the whole length too: a ridge vent drawing from open soffits, with leaks into the attic sealed, holds the deck near outdoor temperature so the edges do not grow ice. A Maynard roof built this way should give its full rated life.

faq.q: Is it a problem to reroof only one side of a Maynard two-family?
faq.a: It is possible, but rarely ideal. A single roof split down the middle needs a careful joint where the new and old sections meet, and that seam is a likely spot for leaks. The shingles may not match, and the warranty may not cover the seam. If the other owner is not ready, talk about timing, since doing the roof as one project gives continuous flashing, venting and a cleaner result.

body: Medfield roughly doubled and redoubled after World War II, and the houses from that stretch, built mostly in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, are where vinyl makes the most sense today. With a Census median build year of 1970 and about 81 percent of homes standing as detached single-family houses, the typical job is a postwar house on its own lot, still wearing its first wood siding or a single replacement layer.

Take that siding off before anything new goes up. Fifty years of paint and weather leave soft spots in the sheathing along sills and at the base of walls, and the only way to find them is to look. Once the wall is bare, damaged boards or plywood come out, a housewrap goes on in overlapping courses, and each window gets new flashing tape with a sloped sill pan. Original paint on most of these houses predates 1978, so the tear-off has to be done under EPA lead-safe practices, with drop cloths, a closed work zone and a thorough cleanup at the end of each day.

Detailing is what makes vinyl look like it belongs. Many Medfield streets mix eras, with a 1960s house a few doors from a much older one, so a modest exposure, a matte finish and trim of reasonable width help a vinyl house sit comfortably among its neighbors. The panels should hang loose on their nails and stop short of the channels so they can grow and shrink with the season. While the old soffit is open, vented soffit panels can go in to help the attic breathe. Ask how the contractor will handle window surrounds and the soffit. Done properly, vinyl lasts twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Will vinyl look out of place on my 1960s Medfield house next to older homes?
faq.a: Not if the details are chosen with care. A traditional lap profile in a muted color, with wide enough corner boards and window trim, reads well alongside older painted houses. Glossy finishes and very narrow trim tend to look thin. Seeing a full panel and a trim sample against your house before you commit, in daylight, is the simplest way to judge how it will look on a mixed Medfield street.

body: Medfield holds some of the oldest wooden houses in the state. The Dwight-Derby House on Frairy Street dates to 1697, the Peak House on Main Street was rebuilt after King Philip's War, and parts of the Lowell Mason house have been tree-ring dated to 1651. On First Period buildings like these, clapboard is part of the structure's record, and any original boards that survive deserve protection rather than replacement.

That means repairing first. Failed clapboards can be cut out one at a time and new ones slipped in at the same exposure, leaving sound original boards in place. Replacement boards should match the original thickness and profile, which on a very old house may require custom milling. Every new board should be primed on all faces and the ends sealed. On houses this old, it is worth talking with a preservation-minded carpenter before taking any original siding down. The National Register listings in town, including the Inness-Fitts House on Main Street, do not on their own restrict owners, but the material is irreplaceable.

Most Medfield clapboard jobs are on newer houses, of course. With only about 13 percent of homes built before 1940, the bigger group is owners of postwar houses who want a traditional painted finish. For them, pre-primed cedar or pine boards over a ventilated rain screen hold paint far longer than boards nailed tight to the wrap. Use stainless or hot-dipped nails and back-prime. Any pre-1978 paint on the walls being stripped requires EPA lead-safe practices. With regular painting, clapboard can last twenty-five to forty years.

faq.q: Can damaged clapboards on an old Medfield house be repaired without losing the originals?
faq.a: Yes, and on a very old house that is usually the better approach. Damaged boards can be cut out individually and replaced with new ones milled to the original profile, primed on all sides and painted to match. Sound original boards stay in place. On a First Period house, ask the contractor to set aside any boards they remove so they can be reviewed before they are discarded.

body: A lot of Medfield owners replacing worn siding on a 1960s or 1970s house choose fiber cement plank. It gives a painted clapboard look without the short repaint cycle of wood, it does not rot, and it resists insects. About 86 percent of Medfield homes are lived in by their owners, and people settled in for the long haul tend to value a cladding rated for thirty to fifty years.

Clearances are where installation goes right or wrong. Fiber cement should not touch soil, roofs, decks or patios, since the boards wick water at cut edges. Hold the bottom edge up off the soil and off every patio, step or deck board, and where a lower roof butts a wall, lift the planks clear of the shingles so they ride over the metal step pieces, ending at a diverter that kicks water into the gutter. This is especially important on lots near the Charles River or wetlands, where the soil stays damp and splash-back can soak the lower boards. Every cut end should be sealed, and every butt joint backed with a flashing strip.

The material is heavy and sharp to cut. Nailing follows the maker's schedule, into studs or sheathing it approves, and cutting is done with electric shears or a vacuum-equipped saw because the dust carries silica. Factory-finished boards reduce painting later. Ask any Medfield contractor how they will handle clearances, dust and flashing, and whether they follow the manufacturer's installation guide, which also protects the warranty. On walls under trees near Rocky Woods or Noon Hill, a light color hides mildew better than a dark one.

faq.q: My Medfield house is near the Charles River. Is fiber cement a good choice?
faq.a: It can be, as long as the installer respects the clearance rules. On damp lots, the bottom boards should stay well above the ground and above any patio or deck, and cut ends must be sealed so they do not absorb water. Good gutters and downspouts that send water away from the house help too. Fiber cement does not rot, which makes it a reasonable choice for wetter sites.

body: Cedar shingles fit across Medfield's range of houses, from older homes near the center to postwar and newer houses whose owners want a natural texture instead of painted lap siding. They are also a good match for houses tucked into the hilly, wooded land around Rocky Woods and Noon Hill, where weathered wood blends with the surroundings.

Those same woods slow drying. A wall that never gets direct sun can hold moisture long after a storm passes, and wet cedar is what feeds mildew, moss and early splitting. Give the courses an air space to work with: a corrugated spacer mat, thin vertical strapping, or a housewrap made with a textured face for shingles. Roof water deserves equal attention, since a gutter that spills down one wall will age that wall years ahead of the rest. Cutting back limbs that brush the house lets light reach the siding.

Decide on the finish up front. Bare cedar goes silver on its own, but in patches, and the north and shaded faces lag behind. A penetrating stain buys a steadier color at the price of a fresh coat now and then, and factory-dipped shingles come coated front, back and edges, which gives the most uniform look. Each shingle takes a pair of corrosion-proof nails, stainless being the safest, set where the next course will hide them, and a slight gap at the sides lets the wood swell after rain. Start the first course a good distance above the planting beds so it never sits in wet mulch. Questions worth putting to any installer: which shingle grade, what goes behind it, and whether corners will be woven or finished with boards. Built to dry, a Medfield cedar wall should give twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Should I stain new cedar shingles on my Medfield house near Rocky Woods?
faq.a: On shaded walls, stain or pre-stained shingles are usually worth considering. Natural cedar in shade can grow mildew and weather unevenly, while a penetrating stain with a mildewcide slows both. Stain does need renewing every several years. Some Medfield owners use natural shingles on sunny sides and accept the uneven graying, which is fine if the look appeals to you.

body: Trim on Medfield houses comes in two very different forms. Postwar homes from the 1950s to 1970s have simple fascia, rake boards and flat casings, while the older homes near the center carry more elaborate cornices, doorway surrounds and wide corner boards. Both kinds rot in the same places, though: window sills, the lower ends of rake boards and the bottoms of door casings, where water sits longest.

On the postwar houses, start by probing those spots with an awl. Soft wood under the paint usually means the problem has been there a while. Replacement pieces in cellular PVC resist rot well in wet locations, but the material expands with heat, so it needs glued joints and the right fasteners. Wood remains a good choice where a profile needs to match. Either way, new trim should be flashed above windows and doors so the same pieces do not fail again within a few years.

On older houses, the approach changes. Original moldings and doorways on houses like those listed on the National Register in town may be worth repairing rather than replacing, with rotted sections cut out and new wood spliced in, or consolidated with epoxy. When a piece must be replaced, have it milled to the original profile. Most trim on homes built before 1978 has lead paint somewhere in its layers, so scraping, sanding or removing it calls for EPA lead-safe practices. Ask a Medfield contractor to show you the damage, explain the cause, and include the fix for the cause in the estimate.

faq.q: Why does the trim on my Medfield house keep rotting at the window sills?
faq.a: Sills sit at the bottom of the window, where water collects and drains slowly, so they are often the first to fail. Missing or failed flashing above the window, a sill that does not slope enough, or paint that has cracked along the joints let water in. Replacing the sill with a rot-resistant material and adding proper flashing usually stops the cycle. Check the gutters above too.

body: A storm drops a limb on the side of the house, or a few boards near the back door go soft. In Medfield, plenty of siding problems are small enough that a careful repair is the right answer. Replacing a few boards, panels or shingles keeps the rest of the wall intact and costs far less disruption than a full re-side.

A repair is also a chance to find out what went wrong. Rot near a window usually comes from failed flashing or caulk. Damage at a roof edge can trace back to a missing kick-out flashing that lets water run down the wall. Siding near the ground can be soaked by splash-back from a downspout or by mulch piled too high. On lots near Hinkley Pond, Kingsbury Pond or the Charles River, damp ground can add to the problem. Fixing the source is part of a lasting repair.

Matching is the hardest part. Vinyl from decades ago may have faded, and wood siding may have a profile no longer stocked. A contractor can look for the closest current match, take pieces from a hidden wall, or have wood milled to fit. On Medfield's very old houses, sound original boards should stay where they are, with only the failed pieces replaced. With about 64 percent of homes in town built before 1980, disturbing old paint beyond a small patch usually means following EPA lead-safe work practices. Ask the contractor to explain what caused the damage before agreeing to the repair.

faq.q: Can a contractor match the siding on my older Medfield home for a small repair?
faq.a: Often, yes. For wood clapboard or shingles, new pieces can be milled or cut to match and then painted or stained to blend in. For vinyl, a close match may be available, or panels can be borrowed from a hidden area. On very old Medfield houses, the goal is to keep as much original siding as possible, replacing only boards that have failed.

body: When siding is failing on most walls of a Medfield house built between the 1950s and the 1970s, full replacement is often simpler than a series of repairs. Peeling paint that will not hold, rot at sills and corners, and leaks around windows usually mean the wall needs more than new boards.

The real work is under the siding. Stripping to the sheathing allows the crew to check for rot, replace damaged sections, and install a continuous housewrap. Windows and doors get new flashing tape and sill pans, which postwar builders rarely used. Rigid foam insulation can be added at this stage, with trim built out to the thicker wall. Because about 64 percent of homes in town were built before 1980, much of the old siding being removed has lead paint, so EPA lead-safe practices, containment and cleanup apply.

Material choice comes afterward. Vinyl, fiber cement, clapboard and cedar shingles each suit different houses and budgets. For the town's oldest houses, such as First Period or 19th-century homes, full removal of original wood siding is rarely the right first step; repair and repainting usually keep more of the house's value. A house from the 1960s, by contrast, has little original material worth saving once its boards are failing everywhere. For an existing single-family home, ask each contractor how they handle hidden rot, how they protect landscaping, and how the new siding will meet the foundation and roof lines. A complete replacement done well lasts thirty to fifty years or more.

faq.q: What should be included in a full siding replacement quote for a Medfield house?
faq.a: A good quote should cover removal of the old siding, lead-safe practices if the house predates 1978, inspection and replacement of damaged sheathing, a new weather barrier, window and door flashing, the new siding and trim, and cleanup. It should also say how hidden rot will be handled and priced. Ask for a product list and a warranty description in writing.

body: Water management on a Medfield lot depends a lot on where the house sits. The Charles River runs along nearly a third of the town, and Hinkley Pond and Kingsbury Pond add more low, damp ground. There, the job of a gutter system is to collect the roof's water and deliver it somewhere it can soak in, rather than adding it to a lawn that is already squishy underfoot.

Seamless aluminum, rolled out in one piece for each run right in the driveway, has no splices to drip and suits the long straight eaves typical of postwar houses. Set a gentle, consistent slope toward each drop outlet, screw the hangers through the fascia into the rafters behind it, and make sure the back lip sits under the drip edge. Medfield winters load a gutter with packed snow and ice, so closer hanger spacing is cheap insurance. Downspout outlets should not dump onto walkways or driveways, where the water freezes into ice patches.

On wooded lots, especially near Rocky Woods or Noon Hill, leaf fall is a real maintenance problem, and gutter guards can cut down on cleaning. Pine needles call for a fine mesh; oak and maple leaves are handled well by simpler screens or hood styles. Check them once or twice a year regardless. If gutters routinely fill with ice, ask about attic insulation and ventilation, since heat loss often causes ice dams that gutters alone cannot fix. When comparing Medfield gutter quotes, ask about size, downspout placement and how water will be carried away from the house. A properly hung aluminum system should see twenty to thirty years.

faq.q: My Medfield yard stays wet near the house. Will new gutters help?
faq.a: Very often, provided the downspouts discharge far from the house instead of at its corners. Extensions or buried pipe that send water toward lower ground that drains keep it from soaking the soil near the house. Soil around the house should also pitch downward as it leaves the foundation. If the yard is near the river or a pond, some dampness may be natural, but roof water should not add to it.

body: Medfield's most famous roof is on the Peak House, which has the steepest pitch recorded for a colonial house in Massachusetts. Most roofs in town are far plainer, set on homes from the 1960s and 1970s, and many are on their second or third set of shingles. That puts a lot of Medfield houses in line for a full replacement.

Strip it to the boards. A tear-off exposes the sheathing so rotted or delaminated sections can be swapped out before anything new is laid, and it is the only honest way to judge a deck that has carried several roofs. Self-adhering membrane belongs at the lower edge of every slope, run high enough to cover the zone over the heated rooms, as well as in each valley and around the chimney. Fresh drip edge on the eaves and rakes and new step flashing at every sidewall should be in the scope; old flashing bent back into place is a common source of callbacks.

Airflow is the other half of the job. Plenty of postwar Medfield attics have a few small soffit vents and nothing at the peak, so heat builds under the deck in winter and melts snow that refreezes at the gutter line. Pairing open soffit intake with a continuous ridge exhaust, then closing the gaps around ceiling fixtures and the attic hatch and topping up the insulation, keeps the roof surface close to outdoor temperature. Older homes near the center tend to have steeper pitches and large brick chimneys, which call for new base and counter flashing and sometimes a small diverter framed behind the chimney. Ask any Medfield roofer how they plan to vent the attic, how they price damaged decking, and whether they nail to the shingle maker's pattern. On a sound, well-vented deck, architectural shingles are rated for twenty-five to fifty years.

faq.q: What shortens the life of a new roof on a 1970s Medfield house?
faq.a: Mostly heat and moisture that the shingles were never meant to handle. A warm attic cooks the shingles from below in summer and drives ice dams in winter, heavy shade keeps the surface damp and mossy, and flashing reused from the old roof tends to leak early. On a 1970s Medfield home, a full tear-off with new flashing, membrane at the edges and a balanced soffit-to-ridge vent system removes most of those risks.

body: Medford tripled in size in the first three decades of the twentieth century, as streetcars and rail lines brought commuters to new streets in places like West Medford, Fulton Heights and South Medford. That boom left the city with block after block of two-families and modest single houses, and the Census median build year still sits near 1942. A lot of those buildings wear their third or fourth paint job over original wood, and vinyl is the most common way owners get off the repainting treadmill.

The two-family is where most Medford vinyl jobs land; roughly a third of the housing is in buildings with two to four units. Those houses usually have a front porch on each floor, deep window casings, and a frieze board under the eaves. The temptation is to bend aluminum over all of it and run panels to the edges, but that flattens the face of the house and leaves hollow pockets where water sits behind the coil. Keeping the wood casings and corner boards, scraping and painting them, and butting the vinyl to them gives a crisper result.

Expect lead paint under anything removed: nearly half the city's homes predate 1940, so the old clapboard almost certainly carries it, and EPA renovation rules require containment on the ground, misting, and a thorough cleanup. Once the old boards are off, look hard at the sheathing near porch roofs and under sills. Panels must hang with room to slide, because a near-coastal climate brings wide temperature swings between a humid August and a January cold snap. If both households in a two-family share the cost, agree on the color and trim plan in writing first.

faq.q: Should the old clapboard come off before vinyl goes on my Medford two-family?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. Stripping the old boards lets the crew see rotted sheathing, add a continuous weather barrier and flash the windows properly, none of which can happen when vinyl is nailed over the existing siding. On a Medford house of that age, the old paint almost certainly contains lead, so removal has to follow EPA lead-safe practices, but that is a reason to do it carefully, not a reason to skip it.

body: Two Medford neighborhoods show what painted wood siding was meant to look like. Along Pleasant Street, the Old Ship Street district holds Federal and Greek Revival homes from the era when Thatcher Magoun and other shipbuilders worked the Mystic, roughly 1803 to 1855. Near downtown, the Hillside Avenue district is a planned subdivision of mostly Queen Anne houses, built between 1875 and 1895, where clapboard on the lower walls meets shingles and decorative boards higher up.

Copying the original is the job. Federal houses tend to have narrow exposures and thin, flat corner boards; Queen Anne houses mix wider boards with belt courses, skirt boards and window hoods. Measure the exposure on each elevation, since builders often tightened it on the front facade. Lumberyard clapboard may be thicker than what came out of nineteenth century mills, so an older Medford house may need a custom-milled profile to blend. Back-prime every board, prime the cut ends again on site, and hang them with stainless ring-shank nails so the heads do not rust through.

Listing on the National Register does not by itself limit an owner, but ask the city whether any local review applies to your address before changing material or detail. With three-quarters of Medford homes built before 1980, and most of the old clapboard painted before 1978, any removal past a few boards follows EPA lead-safe procedures. A narrow vented gap behind new boards helps them dry, which matters on shaded lots near the Fells.

faq.q: Can I match the clapboard on my Hillside Avenue house in Medford?
faq.a: Almost always, though it may take some effort. Pull a loose board or measure one at the bottom of a wall to get thickness, width and the shape of the lower edge. If no stock profile matches, a mill can run a short batch. For a Medford Queen Anne, also note how the clapboard ends against belt courses and window hoods, since those transitions are where a mismatch shows most.

body: Fiber cement plank makes the most sense on Medford's twentieth-century houses, the two-families and single homes built when the city's population climbed past 59,700 by 1930. Owners of those houses often want the painted-board look they started with but are tired of scraping and repainting every several years. Pre-finished planks in narrow exposures sit comfortably on those streets and carry factory color for many years.

These houses have more roof-to-wall joints than they first seem to: front porches on each floor, a back stair enclosure, bay windows with little roofs, and later additions. Every one is a place where fiber cement needs to stop short of the roofing and where water needs a way out. Lay step flashing course by course, leave the gap the manufacturer specifies above the shingles, and add a diverter at each eave end so water does not run into the wall. Joint flashing behind every plank seam and sealed cut edges complete the system.

On a dense Medford block, dust control is a neighbor issue as much as a safety rule. Cutting releases fine silica, so shears or a vacuum-equipped saw, set up away from open windows on the next lot, should be standard practice. The weight of the boards means staging on tall walls rather than ladders, which on narrow side yards may require a neighbor's permission. Lead-safe removal of the old siding comes first on any house built before 1978, which covers most of the city's housing.

faq.q: Is fiber cement too heavy for an old Medford house?
faq.a: Generally not. It weighs more than vinyl or wood, but the load is spread across the wall, and the framing on a typical Medford two-family carries it without trouble. What matters more is the condition of the sheathing and studs, which the crew should check after tear-off. Rotted framing near porch roofs or sills should be repaired before new siding goes on, whatever the material.

body: Some Medford houses were built around wood shingles. The Hillside Avenue district includes Shingle style homes, such as the Bela Warner house put up in the early 1880s, where the shingled walls wrap continuously around curves and corners. Many Queen Anne houses nearby use shingles in gables and on upper stories over clapboard below, often in decorative cuts like fish-scale or diamond patterns. On houses like these, cedar is the only appropriate repair material.

Start by recording the existing pattern: the exposure, how many rows of each cut shape, and whether the corners are woven or butted. A careful installer will lay out new courses to line up with what remains, so the repair does not show. Red cedar is the traditional material; white cedar weathers to a lighter silver. Fancy-cut shingles are still sold or can be cut by hand to match.

Shade and debris are the practical problems. Lots near the Middlesex Fells sit under tall trees, and walls that rarely see sun stay damp, which leads to moss, mildew and early decay. Install over a breathable drainage mat so the backs can dry, fasten with stainless nails that will not streak the wood, and keep the lowest row well above soil and leaf litter. Clean gutters overhead matter as much as the shingles, since overflow keeps the wall wet. Removing old painted or stained shingles from a house built before 1978 calls for EPA lead-safe work practices.

faq.q: Should I replace the shingles on my Medford Queen Anne gable or just repair them?
faq.a: It depends on how many are failing. If most are sound and a few are split or missing, individual shingles can be slipped out and replaced, matched in size and cut. If many are cupped, soft, or loose across the gable, replacement is usually the better choice. Either way, check the flashing and gutters near the gable, since water from above is the most common cause of shingle decay on Medford houses.

body: Trim carries much of the character of Medford's older houses, and on many of them it is the first thing to fail. Queen Anne and Colonial Revival homes along Hillside Avenue have porch posts, spindles, brackets and cornices; Federal and Greek Revival houses on Pleasant Street have pilasters, wide frieze boards and door surrounds; even the plain two-families of West Medford and Fulton Heights carry deep window casings and porch railings on every floor.

Water decides where rot starts: the tops of window sills that have lost their pitch, the bottoms of porch columns, the undersides of porch roofs where a gutter overflows, and the lower edges of corner boards near the ground. Check each with an awl before any siding work. Where only part of a piece is soft, a scarf joint or a dutchman patch can save the rest; where the whole piece is gone, a new one should be milled to match the original profile.

For replacement material, cellular PVC holds up in the wettest spots, such as column bases, sills and porch skirt boards, though it needs glued joints and fasteners spaced for movement. Treated or primed wood with sealed end grain is better for molded profiles that need to match original work. On a two-family with porches stacked two or three high, staging all levels at once saves time and cost. Most of this trim predates 1978, so stripping or sanding requires lead-safe methods and containment.

faq.q: Can someone match the brackets on my Medford Victorian?
faq.a: Yes. A finish carpenter or a millwork shop can copy a bracket from a sound original, using it as a template for new ones in wood or PVC. Bring an intact bracket, or a clear photo with measurements, so the profile is right. In Medford, where many older houses have lost some of their trim over the years, reproducing missing pieces helps restore the look of the house.

body: A lot of Medford siding problems are smaller than they look. A cracked vinyl panel beside the back stairs, a few loose clapboards on a windy corner, a rotted corner board where a downspout empties, or shingles split on a gable can usually be fixed without residing the whole house. The job is to find the extent of the damage, fix the cause, and match the surrounding material. Keeping sound material in place also preserves original wood that would be hard to replace on an older house.

With nearly half the city's homes built before 1940, older houses often carry problems hidden under their siding. Window heads that were never flashed let water into the wall; porch roofs drain back toward the house; old box gutters leak into the cornice and down the wall framing. An assessment should open the damaged area far enough to see whether the wood underneath is sound and to trace the water to its source. Without that step, a patch may last only a season or two.

Matching is easier with wood than with vinyl. Clapboard and shingles can be milled or cut to any profile, and paint can be matched. Older vinyl colors fade or are discontinued, so one option is to move panels from a hidden wall to the visible repair. Any repair on a pre-1978 house that disturbs more than a small area of paint requires lead-safe practices. On a two-family where one owner pays, agree on who handles which side before work starts.

faq.q: How do I know if siding damage on my Medford house is isolated or a bigger problem?
faq.a: Check how far the damage spreads and whether it follows a pattern. Soft wood around one window or below one downspout usually points to a single source. Damage across a whole wall, peeling paint on several sides, or stains inside suggest a broader moisture issue. On an older Medford house, an on-site assessment that probes the wood and checks flashing will tell you which case you have.

body: Taking all the siding off a Medford house built a century ago usually reveals every earlier repair. The original clapboard may be under asbestos shingle, which may be under aluminum or vinyl; windows may have been replaced without new flashing; additions may have been tied in poorly. A full replacement is the chance to fix all of it at once, which is why owners often choose it once paint failure, rot and leaks start appearing together.

With the wall stripped, the crew can replace rotted sheathing, which on older Medford homes is often wide boards, and install a continuous weather barrier. Every window and door should get new flashing tape and a sill pan. Asbestos siding needs licensed removal, and lead paint on the original boards requires EPA lead-safe containment and cleanup. A good estimate breaks out the siding, the trim and a unit price for rot repair, since nobody knows how much sheathing needs replacing until the old layers come off.

On the city's many two-families, coordination is part of the job. Staging may be up for several weeks, and both households live with it, so agree on schedule, material and color before signing. Narrow driveways and side yards affect where dumpsters and lifts can go. With about 54 percent of homes owner-occupied, many two-families have an owner on one floor and tenants on the other, and EPA rules require that tenants get the Renovate Right pamphlet before work disturbs paint.

faq.q: What should a full siding replacement estimate include for an older Medford house?
faq.a: It should list the removal method, including lead-safe and any asbestos work, the new siding and trim materials, the weather barrier, window and door flashing, and a unit price for replacing rotted sheathing or framing. It should also say how debris will be handled and how long the job will take. For older Medford homes, that unit price matters most, since hidden rot is common.

body: Medford's gutter issues depend partly on where the house sits. Homes near the Middlesex Fells on the city's north side live under heavy tree cover, and leaves, seeds and twigs fill gutters more than once a year. Houses near the Mystic River sit lower and need water carried well away from foundations. On the dense blocks of South Medford and Wellington, a downspout discharging into a narrow side yard can soak both houses.

Older houses here may still have wood gutters or built-in box gutters set into the cornice. These look right on a Federal or Queen Anne house, but a leaking box gutter can rot the cornice, the wall framing and the ceiling below. Decide whether to restore the box gutter with a new lining, or replace it with an exterior gutter and rebuild the cornice. Either choice beats leaving a leaking box gutter in place. Whichever route you take, have the roof edge and fascia checked at the same time, since water damage from an old gutter rarely stops at the gutter itself.

For most houses, seamless aluminum in a K-style or half-round profile, pitched toward the outlets and fastened to solid framing, is the practical choice. Guards matched to the debris help on wooded lots near the Fells, and a larger downspout with a cleanout at the base keeps clogs from backing up. Two-families often have porch roofs on each level that need their own gutters, so check that every downspout connects cleanly. Near-coastal winters bring ice that pulls weak hangers loose, so attic ventilation matters too.

faq.q: Should I keep the built-in box gutters on my Medford house?
faq.a: If the house is an older Federal, Greek Revival or Queen Anne, the box gutters are part of its design, and relining them with a modern membrane or metal can keep them working for decades. If the cornice is badly rotted or the lining keeps failing, replacing them with exterior gutters may be more practical. On a Medford house, the main thing is not to leave a leaking box gutter in place.

body: Medford's older roofs fall into two broad types. The Federal and Greek Revival houses of the Old Ship Street district have simple, steep gable roofs, often with brick chimneys. The Queen Anne houses on Hillside Avenue have complex roofs with dormers, towers and several valleys meeting at odd angles. Most of the twentieth-century two-families in between have straightforward gable or hip roofs with porch roofs below.

A complicated roof is where leaks start. Valleys need ice-and-water membrane under the shingles and a clean metal or woven finish; every wall joint needs new step flashing, and turrets or curved sections may call for a different material altogether. Chimneys on older houses often need repointing as well as new step and counter flashing. Before ordering shingles, ask the contractor how many layers are on the roof now, since a tear-off to the deck reveals soft boards and is required once two layers are present.

With a median build year around 1942, many Medford attics were never designed for modern ventilation. A reroof is the time to add ridge venting and open soffit intakes, air seal the attic floor, and add insulation so the roof deck stays cold in winter and ice dams do not form. Ice-and-water membrane along the eaves and in valleys is standard in near-coastal Middlesex County. On a two-family, porch roofs may be low-slope and need a membrane rather than shingles.

faq.q: What can I do about ice dams on my older Medford house?
faq.a: Ice dams form when attic heat melts snow on the roof, which then refreezes at the colder eaves. The lasting fix is to stop that heat loss: air seal and insulate the attic floor, and ventilate the roof with soffit and ridge vents. On an older Medford house, adding ice-and-water membrane along the eaves during a reroof protects against leaks if a dam still forms.

body: In Medway, a vinyl job is very often a second round of vinyl. Close to half the town's roughly 4,800 homes went up in 1980 or later, and many of those subdivisions were sided in vinyl from the start. Thirty or forty years on, the panels have faded on the sunny side, gone chalky to the touch, and in places split where a basketball or a lawn tractor hit them. Owners usually want the same easy-care wall, just with better color and a stiffer panel.

What separates a good re-side from a quick one happens behind the panels. Strip the old vinyl and look at the wrap underneath: on houses of that era it was often stapled up in pieces, torn around windows and never taped. Fix that, add flexible flashing tape around each window and door, and replace any soft sheathing found at the sills. The trim deserves attention too. Narrow stock J-channel around windows can look skimpy, and a wider window surround or a proper corner post gives a plain colonial more depth.

Medway also has a sizable stock of older houses, roughly 54 percent built before 1980, and the rules change on those. Any home from before 1978 may have lead paint on the original wood, so pulling clapboard or trim calls for EPA RRP containment and cleanup. In Medway Village and Rabbit Hill, where many houses date from the nineteenth century, narrow-profile panels and wide trim keep vinyl from flattening the look of a Greek Revival front. Whatever the house, nail through the center of each slot and leave the panel free to slide; that slack is what keeps the wall flat through a hot August and a cold February. Expect twenty to forty years from a good installation.

faq.q: Can new vinyl go over the old vinyl on my 1980s Medway colonial?
faq.a: It can be done, but it is rarely a good idea. A second layer hides whatever is wrong underneath, such as torn wrap, failed window flashing or soft sheathing, and it makes the window and door trim look recessed. Taking the old panels off adds a little time but lets the crew fix the wall and flash the openings properly. On most Medway houses from that period, the strip-off is worth doing.

body: Medway has two concentrations of old clapboard houses, at opposite ends of town. Rabbit Hill, in West Medway around Highland, Main, Franklin and Milford streets, is mostly Federal and Greek Revival homes that grew up near what is now the West Medway Community Church. Medway Village, in the southeast where Holliston Street meets Village Street, holds more than 240 historic buildings put up mostly during the middle and later nineteenth century, when mills ran on the Charles. Roughly 19 percent of the town's houses predate 1940, and a good share of them are in these two districts.

On these houses the siding and trim work as a set. A Federal house typically has narrow, closely spaced boards and slim corner boards; a Greek Revival house has wider corner pilasters and a deep frieze band under the eaves. When replacing boards, measure the exposure in several places, since it can change between the main block and a later ell. Match the board thickness so new work sits flush with the casings. Many walls can be saved by replacing only the failed courses near the foundation and around windows, rather than stripping the whole elevation.

Both districts are on the National Register, which on its own does not restrict what owners do; it is still sensible to ask the town before changing materials. Paint on these walls is almost always older than 1978, so lead-safe practices apply when boards are scraped or pulled. New clapboard holds paint longest when every face is primed before it goes up, it is nailed with stainless fasteners, and it hangs over a thin drainage gap so the back can dry. Painting within a few weeks of installation keeps primed wood from weathering before the finish coat goes on.

faq.q: How much of the original clapboard on my Rabbit Hill house in Medway can be saved?
faq.a: Usually more than owners expect. Damage tends to concentrate on the bottom few courses, under windows and wherever a gutter has overflowed. Those boards can be cut out and replaced with stock milled to the same profile, leaving the sound boards in place. A contractor should probe the wall and mark the bad boards before quoting. Keeping original material where it is solid also keeps the house closer to how it was built.

body: Medway's newer neighborhoods are a natural place for fiber cement. Close to half of the housing dates from 1980 or later, and those colonials and capes often have long, unbroken walls that plank siding covers cleanly. With roughly 86 percent of Medway households owning their place, people planning to stay for years like the combination of a painted lap look, resistance to rot and insects, and finish coats that outlast paint on wood. A good installation should give thirty to fifty years.

In this town the bottom edge of the wall is where planks get into trouble. Village Street runs along the Charles River, Chicken Brook crosses town, and houses on the lower lots near either can have damp soil right up to the foundation. The cement board wicks moisture wherever it has been cut, so the starter course belongs several inches clear of the dirt and of any patio or deck boards, and each sawn end gets a coat of primer or sealant. At a dormer or porch roof, hold the planks up off the shingles and add a diverter flashing at the low corner so spring melt drains away from the board ends.

The material is heavy, rigid and dusty to cut. Find out up front what the crew does about silica: snapping scored boards, using power shears, or running a blade hooked to a HEPA shop vac, and which corner of the yard becomes the cut zone. Each seam between plank ends should have a small metal or membrane tab tucked behind it, and fastener placement has to stay within the maker's guidelines or the warranty may not apply. For the older houses in Medway Village and Rabbit Hill, fiber cement can approximate clapboard if the plank exposure matches the original boards and the corner and window trim keeps its original width; a smooth board looks more appropriate there than a heavy wood-grain texture.

faq.q: We live on a damp lot by the Charles in Medway. Will fiber cement hold up there?
faq.a: Yes, as long as it is kept out of standing water and splash. On low lots near the Charles or Chicken Brook, the first course should start well above the soil, mulch beds should be pulled back from the wall, and gutters should carry roof water away from the foundation. With cut ends sealed and those clearances respected, fiber cement handles damp sites better than wood, since it will not rot.

body: Cedar shingles are not the traditional finish on most of Medway's older houses. The Federal and Greek Revival homes of Rabbit Hill and the mill-era houses of Medway Village were built with painted clapboard, and switching their main facades to shingles changes their character. Where cedar fits well is on a rear ell, a barn or garage, an addition that should read as secondary, or a newer house on a wooded lot where the owner wants a natural wall.

Moisture is the main thing to manage. Lots near the Charles River and Chicken Brook stay damp, and shaded walls on wooded parcels dry slowly after rain. Shingles in those spots last far longer when they sit over a drainage layer, a mesh or furring strip that leaves air space behind them, so the back face dries as fast as the front. Fasteners matter as much: stainless steel nails will not rust and stain the cedar, and each shingle should be held with two of them, set high enough to be hidden by the next row.

Choose the finish before the first course goes up, because each option sets a maintenance pattern. Natural cedar weathers to gray within a few seasons, faster on the south and west walls. A semi-transparent stain slows that and needs renewing every several years. Solid stain or paint gives a uniform color but must be maintained like any painted surface. Factory-stained shingles, coated on all sides before delivery, give the most even start. In Medway's inland climate, with hot summers and freeze-thaw winters, a properly vented, well-nailed shingle wall should last twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Can I put cedar shingles on an addition to my older Medway Village house?
faq.a: That is one of the better uses for cedar on an older Medway house. Shingling an addition or rear ell while keeping clapboard on the main block makes the new part read as secondary, a common pattern on 19th-century houses. Match the trim widths and roof edge details to the original house so the two parts still look related. Because Medway Village is on the National Register, a check with the town before you start is sensible.

body: The older houses in Rabbit Hill and Medway Village get their character from trim more than from siding. Federal houses rely on delicate cornices, thin corner boards and refined door surrounds, sometimes with a fanlight. Greek Revival houses go bolder, with broad pilasters at the corners, a wide frieze band under the eaves and heavy entry surrounds. When these pieces rot, the goal is to reproduce the profile and thickness exactly, usually by splicing a new section into sound wood instead of removing the whole assembly.

Matching an old molding often means custom milling. A carpenter can take a profile from a sound section and have knives ground to copy it, or build up the shape from several stock pieces. Wood is still the right material for these details on a 19th-century house, primed on all faces and back-sealed before installation. Since the paint on Medway's older trim almost certainly predates 1978, scraping or removing it requires lead-safe methods.

On houses built since 1980, which make up close to half of Medway, the trim story is simpler. Finger-jointed pine from that era rots at predictable spots: the bottoms of door casings, garage jambs, corner boards that sit near grade, and window sills. Cellular PVC is a durable replacement in those locations, since it does not absorb water. It does expand and contract with temperature, so long boards need room at the ends and glued scarf joints. Avoid capping rotted trim with aluminum; it traps moisture and hides the decay. Ask the contractor to probe trim before the job and to price replacement rather than coverage.

faq.q: What is the right way to repair a rotted Greek Revival corner pilaster in Medway?
faq.a: Remove only the damaged part, usually the lower section near the ground, and splice in new wood milled to the same width, thickness and molding profile. Prime every face before installing, flash the top of any base block, and keep the bottom off the ground so water cannot wick into it. Full replacement is only needed when rot runs the whole height. On Rabbit Hill houses, keeping original material where possible is worth the extra effort.

body: A cracked panel beside the driveway, a soft board under a kitchen window, or a few courses lifted by wind are common calls in Medway, and none of them requires residing the house. A careful repair addresses the damaged area and leaves sound siding alone. The challenge is making the patch blend in and making sure whatever caused the damage has stopped.

Many Medway homes date from 1980 onward, and the vinyl on them is often from product lines that no longer exist. A new panel that is close in color can still look wrong beside siding that has weathered for decades. A common workaround is the donor panel: weathered pieces are borrowed from a wall nobody looks at, perhaps the side hidden by the shed, and installed where the damage is, while the fresh stock goes up out of sight. Wood houses are simpler, because a mill can reproduce the board shape and a coat of paint evens out the color.

The cause is usually water. Gutters that overflow above a window, a leader that empties right at the sill, bark mulch heaped up to the first course, or an unflashed deck board bolted against the wall are what usually turn up. On lower lots near the Charles River or Chicken Brook, damp ground adds to the problem. Before patching, the source should be found and fixed, and soft sheathing underneath should be cut out. On the older half of Medway's housing, anything from before 1978, cutting into painted boards triggers the EPA lead rules for containment and cleanup. A written estimate should describe the repair, the cause and the fix for both.

faq.q: Why does the siding near my Medway back door keep going soft?
faq.a: Back doors often have a combination of problems: no drip cap over the door, a small roof or deck shedding water onto the wall, and a step or landing that holds splash against the siding. Water gets behind the boards and stays. A lasting repair replaces the soft siding and sheathing and also adds the missing flashing or drip cap and keeps the step from directing water at the wall.

body: A full replacement in Medway looks different depending on when the house was built. On the 19th-century homes of Medway Village and Rabbit Hill, removing the siding may reveal plank sheathing, gaps, little or no insulation and old repairs. On the large share of houses from 1980 onward, the typical findings are torn or missing housewrap and soft sheathing below windows where flashing failed. Either way, the reason for a full job is that problems run across the whole house rather than one wall.

Once the walls are bare, inspect every section of sheathing and itemize the repairs in writing so there are no surprises. Install a weather-resistive barrier lapped shingle-style, with each window and door getting a sill pan and taped flashing. On older houses, a full strip is also a good time to consider blown-in insulation through the open sheathing or a layer of rigid foam on the exterior, keeping in mind that window and door trim will need extension to the new depth. Houses from before 1978, roughly half of Medway's stock, require EPA lead-safe procedures during tear-off.

The new material can follow the house. Painted clapboard or a smooth fiber cement plank suits the older village houses best, and vinyl or fiber cement are practical on the newer subdivisions. With about 86 percent of Medway homes owner-occupied, most owners are choosing for the long term, which favors details like rain screens, sealed cut ends and quality trim. Ask contractors how they protect landscaping and neighboring property, how they schedule work around weather, and how they handle rot found in framing. A clear written scope helps compare bids on equal terms.

faq.q: What problems are usually found when siding comes off a 1970s house in Medway?
faq.a: The most common are water damage under windows where the original flashing was missing or reversed, soft sheathing near the bottom of walls, and little or no weather barrier. Some walls also have gaps in insulation. Painted wood from that era may contain lead, so removal needs lead-safe methods. A good contractor will show you the damage, explain the fix and price it before covering anything back up.

body: Medway's waterways decide where gutter water should go. Village Street winds along the Charles River, Chicken Brook runs through town, and the Great Black Swamp sits in the middle, so a fair number of lots are low and hold water after a storm. On those properties, roof runoff dumped at the foundation has nowhere to go but into the basement or under a slab.

Plan the downspouts first. Each one should discharge to a spot where the ground falls away from the house, using a long extension, a splash pad or a buried solid line that daylights downhill. On flat, low lots, a dry well may be needed. Avoid running downspouts onto driveways or walkways where water will freeze in winter. Along the eave, the trough wants an even fall toward each outlet, stout hidden brackets, and its rear lip sitting beneath the roof's metal edge, otherwise runoff dribbles down the board behind it and rots the fascia.

Size matters on bigger roofs. Many Medway colonials have long eaves and large roof planes, and a standard gutter can overflow at the corners in a summer downpour; a larger gutter and wider downspouts carry more water. Where oaks and maples overhang the roof, a cover keeps most leaves and seed pods out, although none is truly hands-off. Runs made without seams, shaped from a coil in the driveway to the exact length of each eave, need sealant only at corners and drops. Come winter, troughs that fill solid with ice usually mean attic heat is escaping. Put up with care, a seamless aluminum system in Medway is good for twenty to thirty years.

faq.q: Our Medway cellar gets damp after heavy rain. Where should the downspouts send water?
faq.a: Ideally to a point well out in the yard where the land drops. On flatter lots near the Charles, that may take buried pipe running to the edge of the property, or a dry well if the soil drains. At the very least, use extensions several feet long. Look at the soil around the house as well; it should fall away from the foundation. If the cellar stays damp after both fixes, the water table may be the real source.

body: Roof work in Medway splits into two very different kinds of house. On one side are the subdivision colonials and capes, with half of all homes in town standing by about 1976, many now wearing their second set of shingles. On the other are the steep, older roofs of Medway Village and Rabbit Hill, some of which have been redone so many times that nobody knows what lies under the current layer. In both cases the honest approach is to strip everything down to bare boards or plywood, swap out any sheathing that flexes underfoot, and roll fresh underlayment over a solid base.

Leaks rarely start in the open field of a roof. They start where something interrupts it: a valley, the sides of a dormer, the seam where a family room addition butts into the original wall, a plumbing vent, a chimney. Each of those spots deserves new metal on a reroof. Old step pieces are usually rusted, nail-holed or cut for a shingle size that no longer applies. A brick chimney on a village house typically gets fresh base flashing with counter flashing ground into the mortar joints, and a small saddle behind it if the roof above is wide. Where a lower roof ends against siding, a diverter at the bottom keeps the runoff out of the wall.
