Wooded lots add their own work. Oak leaves, pine needles and seed pods fill troughs fast, and a clogged gutter spills onto the siding and soaks the soil it was meant to protect. Guards cut down cleaning, and oversized downspouts clog less often. Pull the old gutter and press on the fascia before hanging new ones; boards behind years of overflow are often soft. Finally, a gutter packed with ice feeds ice dams, so it is worth asking about attic venting at the same time.

faq.q: Do I need gutter guards on a wooded Shirley lot?
faq.a: On many wooded Shirley lots, guards are worth considering. Trees near the rivers and swamps drop leaves and needles that clog gutters quickly, causing overflow onto siding and foundations. Guards reduce how often gutters need cleaning, though they still need occasional checks. Pairing guards with larger downspouts helps prevent clogs. Choose a style suited to the main debris on your lot, since needles and leaves behave differently.

body: A Shirley house built around 1984, the town median, has probably had one roof replaced already or is due for its first. Builders then often used three-tab shingles that curl and shed granules after a couple of decades, and the plywood or OSB under them can swell and lose strength wherever a vent boot or valley leaked. Stripping to bare deck is the only way to find those soft panels and replace them before the new underlayment goes down; walking a roof and feeling for give is a rough guide but not a substitute.

Older roofs in Shirley Village and around the Center need a different eye. A 19th-century frame house may have a steep main roof, a lower ell, a porch roof and one or more brick chimneys, which means many places where water can find its way in. Plank sheathing may need to be overlaid or patched to give nails solid bite. Use fresh step flashing at every sidewall, new counter flashing cut into the chimney mortar joints, and a diverter where each porch or ell roof meets a wall.

Weather and trees decide much of the rest. Inland Middlesex County snow sits on roofs for weeks, then melts from attic heat and refreezes at the overhang, so a self-adhering membrane along each eave and valley is worth the material. A cold, well-vented attic does more, with soffit intake balanced against ridge exhaust and air leaks sealed from below. North slopes under trees near the rivers stay damp and gather moss, so trimming branches and keeping gutters clear helps an architectural shingle roof reach its full life.

faq.q: Why is there moss on the north side of my Shirley roof?
faq.a: Moss grows where shingles stay damp and shaded, which is common on north slopes of wooded Shirley lots near the rivers and swamps. It holds moisture against the shingles and shortens their life. Trimming trees to let in light, keeping gutters clear and improving attic ventilation all help. Gentle cleaning with a roof-safe moss treatment can remove it, but avoid pressure washing, which strips granules.

body: Shrewsbury's median house was built in 1979, which puts the typical vinyl customer here in a raised ranch, a split-entry or a garrison from the postwar decades or the 1970s, often on a lot that tilts. The town sits around 670 feet and the ground is broken up by hills and small streams, so a lot of these houses show one story at the front door and two at the back. That tall downhill wall is where original siding has taken the most weather, and it is also the hardest wall to work on.

Before quoting, a contractor should explain how they will reach that elevation safely: pump jacks or proper staging, not a long extension ladder on sloping grass. They should also show where the starter strip will run, since on a sloping lot the grade drops along the wall and the first course has to clear soil the whole length. Old siding comes off so the sheathing can be checked around the basement-level windows and sliders, which on raised ranches are notorious for missing flashing. A new weather barrier, taped window heads and sill pans go on before the panels.

Vinyl itself is forgiving if it is allowed to move. Nail heads should stop a hair short of the panel, slots should be used in the center, and channels need room at the ends so a long run can grow on a July afternoon. Pick a panel with a decent thickness for the windy hilltop lots. About half of Shrewsbury homes predate 1980, so a tear-off may disturb lead paint and must follow EPA RRP practice. One more check: houses in the local historic district around the Common need Historic District Commission review before any change of siding material.

faq.q: My Shrewsbury raised ranch has a tall back wall. Does that change a vinyl job?
faq.a: Yes, in two ways. First, access: a two-story wall on a slope needs staging or pump jacks so the crew can work safely and install panels straight. Second, water: the lower level of a raised ranch often has sliders and windows that were poorly flashed, and the wall takes splash from the ground and runoff from the deck above. Expect the contractor to spend extra time on flashing and on the starter course there.

body: Shrewsbury's oldest buildings stand around the Town Common, on the old Rocky Plain along what became the Boston Post Road. The First Congregational Church of 1766 is white clapboard, and so are the Federal-era Samuel Haven, Philo Slocum and Jonas Stone houses and the Reverend Joseph Sumner House of 1797, all with multi-pane sash windows set into their walls. The area has been a local historic district since October 1972, and visible exterior changes there go before a Historic District Commission.

If your house is in that district, the first step is a conversation with the commission, before any material is ordered. For the work itself, the goal is to make new boards indistinguishable from the old. That means measuring board exposure, thickness and profile, replicating the corner and casing details exactly, and using wood rather than a substitute unless the commission agrees otherwise. Boards should be primed on all faces, fastened with stainless nails, and painted to match the rest of the facade.

Clapboard is just as much at home on the streetcar-era houses built between 1915 and 1940, when Shrewsbury's population doubled. Many of those streetcar-suburb homes still have their original wood siding under several coats of paint, and only about 11 percent of homes in town are that old, which makes them worth keeping in character. Removing old painted clapboard on any house built before 1978 brings EPA lead-safe rules into play: containment, careful handling of the old boards and verified cleanup. A thin drainage gap behind new boards helps the paint hold on hilltop walls that take the weather.

faq.q: Do I need approval to replace clapboard on my house near the Shrewsbury Common?
faq.a: If the house is inside the local historic district around the Common, visible exterior changes are reviewed by the Historic District Commission, so contact the town before ordering material. Replacing damaged clapboard with matching wood is generally simpler to approve than switching to a different material. Bring photos, measurements and a description of the boards you plan to use. Outside the district, clapboard choices are up to the owner.

body: Shrewsbury has about 15,400 homes, and a large share are mid-century and 1970s houses originally clad in wood or hardboard lap siding. Fiber cement suits those well: it reproduces the painted lap look, will not rot, and holds paint much longer than wood. It is also a solid choice for the houses near Lake Quinsigamond, where paint on wood tends to give out quickly from the moisture and sun bouncing off the water.

The weight of Hardie Plank is the first practical issue in a town this hilly. Each board is heavy, and carrying bundles down a steep driveway or around a house built into a slope takes planning. Ask where the material will be stored, how it will be kept dry and flat, and what staging the crew will use on tall downhill walls. Lake lots often have little room between the water and the wall, which makes both storage and staging tighter still.

Installation details decide how the siding ages. Boards must stay clear of soil, decks and roof surfaces by the manufacturer's spacing, with a gap above step flashing where siding meets a roof. Joints get flashed from behind, and every cut end is sealed before it goes up. Cutting fiber cement releases crystalline silica, so crews should use dust-collecting saws or shears. In the Town Common local historic district, a material change from wood to fiber cement needs Historic District Commission review first; elsewhere in Shrewsbury the choice belongs to the owner.

faq.q: Is fiber cement a good choice for a Shrewsbury house on Lake Quinsigamond?
faq.a: Often, yes. Wood siding near the lake takes moisture and reflected sun, and paint tends to fail sooner there. Fiber cement holds a factory finish far longer and does not rot. The main challenges on a Shrewsbury lake lot are access and storage, since many sit close to the water with little working room. Ask how the crew will stage the walls and protect the shoreline from dust and debris during the job.

body: Cedar shingles have a natural home on the cottages summer residents built along Lake Quinsigamond. Those small, simple houses suit a weathered wall, and many have been winterized and expanded over the years, which often means new siding on additions that should blend with the old part. Shingles also work as an accent on Shrewsbury's later colonials, on a gable or a front porch wall, for owners who want some texture.

Lake houses are hard on cedar. The side facing the water catches sun and wind, while the side facing the street or a hill may sit in shade and stay damp, and the two will weather very differently. A drainage mat or furring behind the shingles lets them dry from the back, which slows cupping and rot. Shingles should be spaced a little apart to allow for swelling, and the bottom course held up off the ground. On lots with only a few feet between the house and the shoreline, the crew needs a plan for keeping debris and stain out of the water.

Up on the higher ground, wind becomes the concern. At about 670 feet, exposed walls on Shrewsbury's hilltops take driving rain and gusts, so fasteners should be stainless, two per shingle, placed where the next course covers them, and the underlayment should be continuous and well lapped. Decide on the finish up front: natural cedar weathers gray at uneven rates, while factory-stained shingles start uniform and hold their tone longer. A well-installed shingle wall can serve twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Why do the cedar shingles on my Shrewsbury lake cottage look so different on each side?
faq.a: Each side gets different weather. The lake side of a Shrewsbury cottage catches sun, wind and reflected light, so shingles there bleach and dry quickly. Shaded sides stay damp and may darken or grow mildew. The difference is normal for natural cedar. To even it out, a bleaching oil or semi-transparent stain can be applied to all walls, and trimming back trees on the shady side helps the shingles dry.

body: The Federal houses around the Shrewsbury Common are a lesson in how much trim matters. The Samuel Haven House has a fanlight and sidelights framing its door, and its neighbors carry cornices, corner boards and window casings sized for the multi-pane sash in their walls. Because the area is a local historic district, replacing any of that trim involves the Historic District Commission, and the expectation is that new work matches the old in profile and material.

On historic trim, the practical approach is to save as much original wood as possible. Rotted sections at the bottoms of door surrounds or corner boards can be cut out and replaced with new wood joined to the sound part. Moldings can be copied by a millwork shop from a sample. Sills that have sagged or lost their slope should be rebuilt so water runs off instead of soaking into the casing. Most of these houses carry many layers of lead paint, so scraping and stripping follow EPA RRP rules.

Newer Shrewsbury houses have a different set of failures. On the town's many 1970s homes, the water table board at the base of the wall, window sills, and fascia behind gutters are the first pieces to go, especially on downhill walls where runoff concentrates. Garage door jambs also rot from splash and snow. Cellular PVC or composite trim cuts down on repainting and resists rot in those spots, as long as it is fastened to allow for movement and the joints are flashed rather than caulked. Ask whether a contractor plans to replace rotted trim or cover it in aluminum.

faq.q: Can I use PVC trim on my house in the Shrewsbury historic district?
faq.a: That decision rests with the Historic District Commission, which reviews visible exterior changes around the Town Common. Some commissions accept PVC on certain parts, such as hidden areas or the bottom of corner boards, while asking for wood on prominent features like door surrounds. Bring drawings or photos and samples to the conversation before ordering. Outside the district, PVC is a common choice for water-prone trim on Shrewsbury houses.

body: Plenty of Shrewsbury houses call for a fix rather than a full re-side. Half the homes in town went up in 1979 or later, and on many of those the cladding is still mostly sound, with trouble confined to one wall or one corner: panels split in a winter storm, a strip ripped off a gable by wind on a hilltop lot, boards going soft just above the foundation. A focused repair can keep such a wall serviceable for a long while yet.

On hillside property the damage usually tells a drainage story. Runoff from the slope above, or from a driveway pitched toward the garage, can sheet against one face of the house all spring, and that face rots first. Raised ranches and split-levels collect splash at their lower walls from patios and from decks that drip onto them. Lake Quinsigamond lots add damp air and shade. A repair is only worth paying for if the water problem is handled with it, whether that means regrading, longer downspout runs, a diverter where a roof edge dies into the wall, or proper flashing for a deck ledger that was simply bolted on.

Getting the patch to blend comes next. Sun-faded vinyl can be traded for pieces off a wall that faces the woods, and a millwork shop can reproduce an old wood clapboard. If the house is in the Town Common local historic district, swapping visible original material for something new needs the Historic District Commission first. About 51 percent of the town's homes predate 1980, so a repair that scrapes or cuts painted wood on a pre-1978 house beyond a minor area falls under the federal RRP lead rule. Snapshots of the damage sent ahead help the estimator plan.

faq.q: Why does the siding rot on just one side of my Shrewsbury house?
faq.a: Almost always because that side gets more water. On a sloped Shrewsbury lot, runoff from higher ground or a driveway pitched toward the house can keep one wall soaked. A roof edge that ends against the wall with no diverter, a gutter spilling over, or garden soil heaped against the lowest boards will do the same. Sort out the drainage before new boards go on, or the replacements will rot in turn.

body: About half of Shrewsbury's roughly 15,400 homes were built before 1980, and roughly 72 percent are owner-occupied, so many owners are now looking at houses where siding, trim and window flashing have all worn out at once. A full re-side makes sense when patching has turned into a yearly chore: paint failing on several walls, soft trim at many corners, and water stains inside below windows.

The work begins with removing the old siding to the sheathing. Damaged sheathing is replaced, and a weather-resistive barrier is installed continuously, lapped so water drains outward. Each opening is re-flashed, pans under the sills first and tape lapped over them. Open walls also invite a layer of foam board, though the casings around windows and doors then have to be built out. Sheathing on houses of that age might be boards, plywood or fiberboard, and each fails in its own way, so it deserves a careful look. On houses built before 1978, removal follows EPA RRP lead-safe rules with containment and cleanup.

Hilly lots complicate the logistics. Dumpsters may have to sit on a steep driveway, debris needs protecting from runoff, and downhill walls need proper staging. Lake lots near Quinsigamond often have little room on the water side. Inside the Town Common local historic district, the Historic District Commission reviews visible exterior changes, so a re-side there starts with the commission, especially if the material will change. Outside the district, owners pick freely among the usual claddings. Get each bidder's plan for hidden rot, staging and protecting the yard on paper.

faq.q: What should I ask before a full siding replacement on my Shrewsbury hillside house?
faq.a: Find out what staging goes on the tall downhill wall, where the dumpster and material pallets will sit on a sloped lot, and what keeps nails and scraps out of swales and streams. Request a unit price for any rotted sheathing uncovered, and whether new flashing and a weather barrier are included. If the house is near the Shrewsbury Common, confirm whether Historic District Commission review applies before choosing materials.

body: Water moves fast in Shrewsbury. The town sits around 670 feet, the ground is hilly and cut by small streams, and many houses are built into slopes. A heavy rain sends runoff across lawns and down steep driveways, and any downspout that empties at the foundation on the uphill side is adding to water that is already headed for the basement.

Decide where every downspout ends before choosing the gutters. On the high side of a sloped lot, the outlet should drop into buried solid pipe that runs around the house and releases the water well below the foundation. On the low side, an extension or splash block should put water on lawn, not on a walk or driveway that turns to ice overnight. Big roofs on colonials and raised ranches can overwhelm a standard trough in a summer thunderstorm; a wider gutter and larger leaders are cheap insurance.

Leaves come next. The wooded streets and the lots around Lake Quinsigamond shed foliage and needles every fall, and a guard suited to what actually falls on that roof cuts the number of ladder trips. Seamless aluminum, rolled out to length in the driveway, fits most Shrewsbury houses. Some older homes still carry wooden gutters; those usually need fascia repair first, and near the Common any visible change goes before the Historic District Commission. Before any new gutter goes up, push a screwdriver into the fascia, because soft wood behind the brackets will let go under the first heavy load of winter ice.

faq.q: My Shrewsbury driveway ices up below the downspout. What can be done?
faq.a: Redirect the downspout so it no longer empties onto the driveway. One option is a length of buried pipe that crosses under the pavement and lets the water out on the lawn below; another is shifting the leader to a different corner of the house. On sloping Shrewsbury lots, a little planning keeps water off paved surfaces where it refreezes. Also check whether ice dams on the roof are sending extra meltwater into the gutter.

body: Sitting near 670 feet, Shrewsbury catches more snow and harder freezes than the lower towns toward Boston, and its roofs show it. The 1979 median build year means the typical house went up during the 1970s, so the roof overhead is likely the second or third one, sometimes installed right over the first. A Shrewsbury reroof is often the first chance in decades to see the actual boards under all that asphalt.

Strip it completely. Layered roofs trap heat, hide soft decking, and add weight the rafters were never sized for. Once the sheathing is bare, rotten panels get replaced, then a rubberized ice shield is rolled out across the lower roof edge and down the valleys, the places where Shrewsbury snow packs in and refreezes night after night. Raised ranches and split-levels, common in town, have spots where a short roof butts into a taller wall. Those joints want fresh step flashing tucked under each course of siding, plus a small diverter at the lowest point so water drops into the gutter. Chimney flashing should be cut into the mortar joints, not just glued on.

Under the roof, the attic decides how long the shingles survive. Air should enter through open soffit vents and leave through a ridge vent, and the ceiling below should be sealed and insulated so household heat stays out of the attic. When that balance is right, snow melts off a cold deck slowly and ice dams have little to feed on. Lake Quinsigamond houses take gusts across open water, so ask about a wind-rated shingle and six nails per shingle instead of four. Near the Town Common, visible roofing changes may go before the Historic District Commission. Quality architectural shingles on a sound, vented deck carry a rated life of twenty-five to fifty years.

faq.q: Does a Shrewsbury lake house need a different roof?
faq.a: It usually benefits from a few upgrades. Houses on Lake Quinsigamond take wind straight off the water, which can lift shingle edges. Choose a shingle with a high wind rating, ask for the extra nailing the maker specifies for windy sites, and make sure the starter strip along the eaves and gable edges is the adhesive type. The lake does not spare Shrewsbury its snow, so ice barrier and good attic airflow still matter.

body: In Somerville, the typical vinyl job is a triple-decker or a two-family, not a single house. More than half of the city's units, about 55 percent, are in buildings of two to four units, and only about a third are owner-occupied, so many of the people asking about vinyl are landlords or owner-occupants who rent out the other floors. For them, the appeal is simple: no more scraping and painting three stories of wall every several years, and no more renting staging to do it.

Height changes the installation. A triple-decker wall can run thirty feet or more from foundation to cornice, and vinyl expands and contracts along that whole length. If the panels are nailed tight, the wall shows waves and bulges by the first summer. Each panel should hang on nails left slightly proud, centered in the slots, with clearance at the ends and in every J-channel. Tall walls also face more wind at the top floor, so a thicker panel with a reinforced nailing hem is worth asking about, and the starter strip has to be dead level or every course above it will drift.

The details are where older buildings either keep or lose their character. Many Somerville buildings, with a median build year around 1938, still have bay windows with paneled skirts, window hoods, bracketed cornices and porch trim. Wrapping all of that flat in aluminum coil erases it. A better plan keeps and repaints the original trim, or rebuilds it in PVC at the same size, and runs the vinyl up to it. The original clapboard underneath almost certainly has lead paint, so tear-off follows EPA RRP rules, with containment that protects the building next door.

faq.q: Will vinyl siding on my Somerville triple-decker look wavy?
faq.a: It should not, if it is installed correctly. Waviness on tall walls usually comes from panels nailed too tightly, from an uneven wall underneath, or from thin panels. Each nail belongs mid-slot with a little play under the head, and low spots in an old wall should be shimmed flat before panels go up. A thicker panel resists distortion better. Ask to see a finished triple-decker in Somerville or a nearby city before choosing a contractor.

body: Somerville has more surviving 19th-century wood siding than people expect. About 59 percent of its housing predates 1940, and the Spring Hill historic district alone holds Greek Revival houses from the 1840s alongside Italianate, Gothic Revival and Queen Anne homes. Bow Street in Union Square and Mt. Vernon Street in East Somerville have National Register districts too. On these buildings, painted clapboard is the original wall, and replacing it means matching what was there.

Matching starts with measurements. Record the exposure on each wall; older houses often used narrower boards on the front than on the sides. Note whether the boards have a bead along the bottom edge and how they meet the corner boards and window trim. New clapboard should be clear cedar or pine, primed on every face and end before it goes up, and fastened with stainless or galvanized nails. Where the original boards are still sound, scraping and repainting them, and replacing only the failed ones, often costs less and keeps the house's character.

Clapboard work here comes with two complications. First, lead: almost every painted board on these buildings carries lead paint, so removal, scraping and sanding follow EPA RRP practices, and on Somerville's narrow lots that means containment that keeps dust off the neighbor's windows, cars and garden. Second, review: if the house is in one of the National Register districts, ask the city whether local review applies before changing materials. Listing by itself does not restrict owners. On the many two-families and triple-deckers, clapboard over a rain screen is a good choice for owners who want a traditional look.

faq.q: Is it worth keeping the original clapboard on my Spring Hill house in Somerville?
faq.a: Often, yes. Old-growth clapboard is usually denser and more stable than new lumber, and if most boards are sound, scraping, priming and painting them, with failed pieces replaced to match, preserves the house's character. Lead paint is almost certain, so the work must follow lead-safe practices. If many boards are split or rotted, replacing whole walls with new clapboard milled to the same profile may make more sense. Ask the city about any review before changing materials in Somerville's historic districts.

body: Fiber cement has one advantage that matters more in Somerville than almost anywhere else: it does not burn. In a city of about 4.1 square miles packed with wood-framed two-families and triple-deckers, often separated by a narrow side yard, a noncombustible cladding is worth considering, and it gives the painted lap look of the original clapboard with a much longer repaint cycle than wood.

The challenge is getting it onto the wall. A bundle of planks weighs far more than the same area of vinyl or cedar, and carrying it up three floors calls for pipe scaffold or pump jacks; in a side yard barely wider than a person, that frame may have to stand partly on the abutter's land, which needs their consent. Every cut releases respirable silica, so on these blocks the saw should be vacuum-shrouded or replaced by shears, and the cutting table kept on the street side or in the back yard, well away from the windows of the building next door. Factory-finished boards help here, since they eliminate a second round of staging for painting.

On older buildings, the details take more thought. The new planks stand proud of the old clapboard line, so casings and corner boards often have to be furred out for the planks to finish cleanly against them. The boards need clearance above porch roofs, rear decks and the ground, and every butt joint should have flashing behind it. With about 80 percent of Somerville's housing built before 1980, removing the old siding falls under EPA lead-safe rules. On rental buildings, tenants need notice about staging, noise and access. Find out up front which walls the crew can reach from your own lot and which depend on a neighbor.

faq.q: How do contractors install fiber cement on a Somerville triple-decker with almost no side yard?
faq.a: It takes planning. Crews often use narrow scaffolding or pump jacks that fit in tight spaces, and they may need the neighbor's permission to set staging on their side. Boards are cut away from the building, with dust collection, and carried to the wall. Talk to your neighbors early. In Somerville's dense blocks, a contractor's plan for access and protecting adjacent property is as important as the siding itself.

body: Shingles are part of Somerville's older housing. Queen Anne and Shingle Style houses in the Spring Hill historic district often used cedar in their gables, upper floors and towers, sometimes in decorative patterns. Even many triple-deckers built in the early 1900s had shingled sections at the top or on bays. Replacing those sections with cedar keeps the building's original design.

Somerville's density creates a specific problem for shingles. The side walls between closely spaced buildings get little sun and almost no breeze, so they stay damp long after a rain. Shingles on those walls tend to grow mildew, cup and rot faster. Installing new shingles over an air gap, with a drainage mat or thin furring strips, gives them a chance to dry from behind. Working gutters and downspouts above those walls also matter, since overflowing water often runs down the narrow side yard walls.

Patterned shingles, such as fish-scale or diamond shapes, should be copied exactly, matching the exposure and pattern of the original. Each shingle should be fastened with two stainless nails hidden by the course above. Leave small gaps between shingles for expansion. Old painted or stained shingles on Somerville's pre-1978 buildings almost certainly contain lead, so removal follows EPA RRP practices, including containment that protects neighbors. On a multi-unit building with tenants, plan staging and access around their schedules. Painted shingles suit many older houses; stained ones are lower maintenance where the original finish allows.

faq.q: Why do the shingles on the side of my Somerville house rot faster than the front?
faq.a: Side walls between close buildings get little sun or air, so they stay wet much longer after rain. Gutters overflowing into narrow side yards make it worse. When replacing those shingles, install them over an air gap so they can dry from behind, and make sure the gutters and downspouts above are working. In Somerville's dense neighborhoods, a stain with mildew resistance can also help on shaded walls.

body: Somerville's two-families and triple-deckers carry more trim than their plain reputation suggests. Bay windows often have paneled skirts and brackets, front porches stack two or three levels with columns and railings, cornices carry brackets or dentils, and older houses in Spring Hill have window hoods and corner pilasters. Trim is where most of the character in these buildings lives, and it is also where rot shows up first.

The rear porches are usually the worst. Many Somerville buildings have stacked back porches serving each unit, and their posts, railings, floor edges and the trim where they attach to the house take a beating from weather and use. Front porch columns rot at the base. Bay window sills and skirts catch water. Window hoods on upper floors may hide decay that only shows when the paint is scraped. All of these should be checked before any siding work, because covering rotted trim just hides the problem.

When pieces are replaced, match the original profiles: a mill can reproduce brackets, casings and moldings. Cellular PVC or composite stock works well on upper floors, where repainting is hard and expensive, and on porch parts that stay wet, though it needs proper fastening and expansion allowance. Primed wood is still good for complex moldings. With about 59 percent of the housing built before 1940, almost all old painted trim carries lead, so removal, scraping and sanding fall under EPA RRP rules. On a rental building, plan the work around tenants, who may lose porch access for a time.

faq.q: Can the rotted trim on the upper floors of my Somerville triple-decker be replaced without staging the whole building?
faq.a: Sometimes. If the damage is limited to a few pieces, a lift or a section of scaffolding may be enough. If the cornice, bays and window trim are failing on several floors, it often makes sense to stage the whole wall once and fix everything together, since setting up staging is a big part of the effort. Replacing upper-floor trim with PVC reduces future painting. Lead-safe practices apply on older Somerville buildings.

body: On a Somerville multi-family, siding damage is usually local: a porch corner where water has been running for years, clapboards rotted under a leaking bay window, shingles blown off a top-floor gable, or a section hit by a falling branch or a delivery truck in a tight driveway. These can usually be repaired without re-siding the whole building, which matters when staging three stories is a big part of any job.

Matching the existing siding is the hardest part on older buildings. Clapboard and shingles can be milled or cut to match the original profile, then painted to blend. Vinyl and aluminum added in the mid-twentieth century are harder, since many profiles are discontinued and colors have faded; a contractor may move pieces from a hidden wall to the damaged area. On a two-family where the front is original wood and the sides have been covered, the repair should match each surface.

Each repair should find the source of the water. Rear porches often lack flashing where they meet the house. Bay windows can leak at the roof or sill. Downspouts that dump water into narrow side yards keep the lower siding wet. On Somerville's hills, such as Winter Hill, Spring Hill or Prospect Hill, runoff can hit the uphill side of a building. While the wall is open, check and replace soft sheathing. With most buildings built before 1978, EPA lead-safe practices apply to even small repairs on painted siding. On rental properties, give tenants notice about access and work hours.

faq.q: What does a siding repair on my Somerville two-family involve if tenants live there?
faq.a: The work itself is mostly outside, but tenants will notice noise, crews near windows and porches, and possibly limited access to doors or parking. Give them written notice of the schedule. If the building was built before 1978, lead-safe rules require containment and cleanup, which also protects tenants and neighbors. A clear scope from the contractor, separating repair, trim and any rot work, helps owners and tenants in Somerville know what to expect.

body: Residing a Somerville triple-decker or two-family is largely an access project. These buildings stand three stories tall, often with only a few feet to the next building, and the work needs scaffolding or lifts, a place for the dumpster, and sometimes a street or sidewalk permit if they occupy public space. Neighbors need to agree to any staging on their side, and their cars, windows and gardens need protection.

Under the current siding there is usually a history. Many Somerville buildings, with a median build year around 1938, had their original clapboard covered with asbestos-cement shingles, aluminum or vinyl over the decades. Each layer has its own removal rules: asbestos should be tested and handled properly, and the original painted wood falls under EPA lead-safe rules. Once the walls are stripped, sheathing and framing can be inspected, especially around rear porches and bay windows where water often gets in. Rotted boards are replaced, a weather barrier goes on, and windows and doors are flashed.

Material choice usually comes down to vinyl or fiber cement for low upkeep, or wood clapboard for owners who want an authentic look. Fiber cement offers better fire resistance, which matters on dense blocks. Whatever the choice, keep or rebuild the trim at its original size so the building does not lose its character. With only about a third of homes owner-occupied, many replacements happen on rental buildings, so plan around tenants. Ask for a written estimate that separates siding, trim and rot repair, and ask how the contractor will handle the walls facing neighbors.

faq.q: Do I need my neighbor's permission to reside my Somerville triple-decker?
faq.a: If the staging, ladders or crew need to stand on the neighbor's property, yes. On many Somerville lots, the side walls cannot be reached any other way. Talk to the neighbor early, explain the schedule and how their property will be protected, and get their agreement in writing. If the work needs sidewalk or street space, check with the city about permits. A contractor experienced in dense neighborhoods can help plan access.

body: Gutters on a Somerville building have to deal with two things: tight lot lines and hills. With houses close together, roof water often lands next to the neighbor's foundation or in a shared driveway. On the slopes of Winter Hill, Spring Hill, Prospect Hill or Clarendon Hill, water that reaches the ground keeps moving downhill, sometimes into the basement of the building below.

The answer is careful routing. Each leader should empty onto your side of the line, clear of foundations, walkways and driveways, where water can freeze into a hazard. Where there is no room on the ground, a downspout can be connected to underground pipe if the site allows, or extended along the building to a better outlet. On a triple-decker, a downspout running three stories needs secure straps and a properly sized outlet, since a long run carries a lot of water fast.

A triple-decker's main roof is often nearly flat and pitched toward the rear, so the only gutter may run along the back eave, or the roof may empty through a scupper into a leader box. Keep those openings free of leaves and grit, because a blocked scupper sends water over the cornice. Where a hung gutter is used, a seamless run cut to length avoids leaky seams, and it should fall steadily toward its outlet, fastened by concealed brackets screwed into solid wood and lapped under the roof edge metal. With about 55 percent of units in two- to four-family buildings, the stacked rear porches usually have small roofs that need gutters of their own. Any soft fascia should be replaced first, and the crew should explain how it will work safely at third-floor height.

faq.q: Water from our Somerville downspout runs into the neighbor's driveway. How is that usually solved?
faq.a: The goal is to keep your roof water on your own lot. A contractor might relocate the leader to a different corner of the building, run it horizontally along the wall to your side, or tie it into a buried pipe where the yard allows. Sometimes splitting one long gutter into two shorter runs with separate outlets fixes it. On a tight Somerville lot, it helps to look at the whole roof and both buildings before deciding.

body: Many Somerville triple-deckers and two-families have flat or low-slope roofs hidden behind a cornice, while older houses in Spring Hill and the other historic districts have steep gable, mansard or Queen Anne roofs. Sort out which you have before collecting bids. A near-flat triple-decker roof is covered with a sheet or torch-applied membrane, rubber, thermoplastic or modified asphalt, and the job turns on drainage toward the back and how the membrane wraps the cornice. The pitched roofs take asphalt shingles, laid after stripping the old layers to the boards.

Access shapes the job more here than almost anywhere. A three-story building with narrow side yards and neighbors close on both sides means materials have to be lifted to the roof, often by conveyor or crane, and debris has to come down safely. Ask how the contractor will protect adjacent roofs, cars and windows, and where the dumpster will go. On attached buildings, flashing at the joints between roofs needs close inspection.

The typical building in the city dates to about 1938 and has usually worn three or four roofs already, and the boards beneath may be stained or soft wherever a chimney or dormer leaked. Brick chimneys on these buildings are often tall and exposed, and they need fresh flashing cut into the mortar joints, not tar smeared over old metal. On pitched sections, self-adhering membrane goes along each eave and down each valley. Old attics here are rarely vented; opening the soffits, adding a ridge vent and sealing and insulating the top-floor ceiling help prevent ice from building at the eaves. Top-floor tenants need notice, since roofing is noisy and the crew may need attic access.

faq.q: Our Somerville triple-decker has a nearly flat roof behind the cornice. What should go on it?
faq.a: A low-slope membrane, not shingles, which cannot shed water at that pitch. Rubber, thermoplastic and modified asphalt sheets all work when seamed and flashed properly. The roofer should confirm the roof drains toward the back, clear or rebuild any scupper, and detail where the membrane turns down over the cornice, since that edge is where Somerville flat roofs most often leak into the top-floor walls.

body: Southborough did most of its building late. Manufacturing faded once the reservoirs went in, and serious growth did not start until the 1970s, which is why the Census puts the median home at 1981. Those houses, mostly large single-family colonials and contemporaries on wooded lots, are the ones now coming up for new siding, and vinyl is often the first material their owners price.

The panels are rarely the weak link. Builders in that period commonly used fiberboard or thin plywood sheathing and skipped house wrap, or stapled it on loosely with no thought for laps. Window flashing was often a bead of caulk. When the old siding comes down, plan to wrap the whole house, tape every window and door opening from the sill up, and install head flashing that sheds water over the casing. Soft fiberboard at the corners or under windows should be cut out and replaced with plywood before anything is nailed to it.

The long, plain walls of a two-story colonial show every ripple, so panel choice matters. A thicker panel, or one with a rigid foam backer, spans small hollows and stays straighter in summer sun. Get the J-channel sized for the panel thickness, leave room at every end for expansion, and hang panels loosely rather than nailing them tight. About half of Southborough houses were built before 1980, so tear-off on the older half should follow lead-safe practices for pre-1978 paint. For the nineteenth-century buildings in Cordaville or near Main Street, consider whether vinyl suits the house at all before committing.

faq.q: What should a vinyl siding quote include for my 1980s Southborough colonial?
faq.a: Beyond the panels, it should list removal of the old siding, replacement of any soft sheathing, a full house wrap with taped seams, flashing tape at each window and door, new J-channel and corner posts, and how trim will be handled. On a Southborough colonial of that era, the wall underneath often needs more attention than the siding, so make sure every bid covers those items the same way before comparing totals.

body: Two pockets of Southborough still show what painted clapboard looked like here a century and more ago. In Cordaville, Milton Sanford started building houses for his mill hands on Parker and Cottage Streets after 1847, and along Main Street between the Fay School grounds and Latisquama Road, the center holds an 1870 Italianate town house among late nineteenth-century civic and church buildings. Only about one home in nine predates 1940, so these streets account for much of the old wood siding in town.

Repairs on those houses work best when nobody can tell where the old boards end. Record the visible reveal, the board thickness and the way each course meets the corner boards before stripping anything. Worker housing tended to be plain, with narrow trim, while houses near the center may have wider casings and corner pilasters; copy whichever is there. Sound old boards pulled from a back wall can patch a front elevation if a close match is hard to find.

The wood should be clear and stable, primed on all faces and cut ends before it goes on. A thin ventilated gap behind the siding lets moisture escape and makes each paint job last longer, a real benefit on shaded walls. Use corrosion-resistant nails, and keep the lowest course above grade. Any pre-1978 paint is presumed to contain lead, so scraping, sanding or removing old clapboard falls under EPA RRP rules. The center became a National Register district in 2021; that listing on its own does not limit owners' choices. On newer Southborough houses, real clapboard is an appearance decision that comes with a repainting commitment.

faq.q: How can I keep the old character of my Cordaville worker house in Southborough when replacing siding?
faq.a: Keep the same simple profile and reveal the house had. Many Cordaville workers' houses on Parker and Cottage Streets were plainly finished, so the narrow corner boards and window casings matter as much as the boards. Measure what is there, match it in primed wood, and avoid adding decorative trim that was never part of the design. If the original siding survives under a later layer, it is the best guide.

body: On the bigger late-twentieth-century houses that make up most of Southborough, fiber cement is the material owners pick when they want painted boards without the painting. Baked-on color from the plant lasts far longer than a site paint job, the boards are immune to rot and carpenter bees, and they lie flat across the tall, broad elevations of a two-story house. Since roughly 88 percent of households here own their homes, plenty of buyers are planning for the long haul, and a cladding meant to last thirty years or more fits that thinking.

Where the planks stop matters as much as where they go. Leave daylight between the first board and the soil, and give it extra room on lots that fall toward wetlands or the Sudbury Reservoir, where wet ground and rain splash linger. Hold the siding up off any deck, and where a second-floor wall climbs above a garage or porch roof, end the boards short of the shingles, slip step pieces beneath, and turn the water out with a diverter at the bottom. Slide a small piece of flashing behind each seam between board ends, and paint or seal every edge a saw has touched.

Weight is the other difference from vinyl. The boards want firm sheathing and nails that reach the framing, and some 1970s houses with soft fiberboard will need a plywood layer first. Sawing the product throws off fine silica, which is a lung hazard, so the crew should rely on shears or saws hooked to a vacuum and keep the cutting station outdoors and downwind of open windows. Ask how cut ends on pre-finished boards will be touched up, what trim material will be used at corners and openings, and whether the warranty covers both the boards and the finish.

faq.q: Is fiber cement a sensible choice for a Southborough home next to wetlands?
faq.a: Yes, provided the installation is planned around moisture. Beside wetlands or reservoir land in Southborough, start the first board high off the soil, pitch the yard so it drains outward, and run downspouts far enough out that roof water never pools against the walls. Fiber cement will not rot, but trim, sheathing and framing behind it can, so the drainage layer and flashing are what protect the house.

body: Many Southborough houses sit on wooded lots that back onto reservoir land or open space like Breakneck Hill, and cedar shingles suit that setting. Untreated cedar slowly weathers to gray and blends with trees and stone walls. On a contemporary or a cape, shingles can cover the whole house; on a colonial, they are sometimes used on gables or an addition to break up long walls.

The trade-off is drying time. Under heavy shade, cedar stays wet after rain and dew, which invites mildew and, over time, decay. A rain screen, a mesh or furring layer that leaves an air gap behind the shingles, lets them dry from both sides and adds years to their life. Start the first course several inches up from the mulch beds and any deck. Put a metal cap over each window and door, and nail with stainless so the fasteners never bleed dark marks down the courses.

Color is worth planning. Raw cedar weathers unevenly at first, with sheltered spots under the eaves staying darker and the sunny side turning gray first, and that blotchy stage can last a few years. Shingles dipped in stain before delivery skip that awkward phase and look uniform right away. A penetrating stain renewed on schedule also slows weathering. Ask contractors whether the corners will be woven or butted against boards, how they will detail walls that face the woods and stay damp, and how they will protect plantings during installation on a heavily landscaped Southborough lot.

faq.q: Why do new cedar shingles on a Southborough house look blotchy?
faq.a: New cedar weathers at different rates depending on sun, rain and shade. On a wooded Southborough lot, one wall may stay darker under the trees while another grays quickly, and areas under the eaves change more slowly. That uneven stage usually evens out over a few years. Owners who dislike the patchy look can order factory-stained stock, or brush on a penetrating finish within the first season.

body: The center along Main Street is a good lesson in how trim defines a building. The 1870 Italianate town house and the late nineteenth-century churches and civic buildings nearby rely on cornices, brackets, window heads and corner treatments for their character. On older houses close to the center, rotted trim should be copied in width, depth and profile; a stock board from the lumberyard will look flat and out of place.

Most trim work in Southborough is on newer houses, though, and there the problems are mechanical. Corner boards rot at the bottom where rain splashes up, door casings and garage jambs soak up meltwater, and window sills on the weather side fail first. Original trim on many 1980s houses was finger-jointed pine primed only on the face, and it rots from the back or the end grain. Water is usually being directed onto these pieces by a missing drip cap, an overflowing gutter or a deck ledger without flashing.

Replacing the wet-zone pieces with cellular PVC or a primed composite, and adding head flashing above each one, breaks the cycle. Plastic trim grows in summer, which is why long lengths are bonded at the seams and pinned on the schedule the maker prints. Drier pieces higher up can often stay and be repainted. On an older house, a decayed stretch of molding can be cut back to sound wood and pieced in. Be cautious about aluminum wrapping, which traps moisture against existing wood and hides rot. Ask the contractor to identify the cause of each failure and include the fix in the scope.

faq.q: Should I replace all the trim on my 1980s Southborough house or just the rotted parts?
faq.a: Usually just the rotted parts, plus anything that will be covered by new siding. On a Southborough house from the 1980s, the lower corner boards, door casings, garage jambs and weather-side sills tend to fail first, while upper trim often stays sound. Replacing those pieces with PVC and fixing the water source is economical. If most pieces are soft or you are re-siding anyway, a full trim replacement makes sense.

body: Southborough's wooded lots generate a steady stream of small siding repairs. A falling branch cracks a few vinyl panels, a string trimmer chews the lowest course, a strong wind lifts a section at a gable, or a board near a downspout softens. Each of these can usually be fixed on its own, without the expense of re-siding the house.

Matching takes some judgment. On many early-1980s houses, the original vinyl color or profile has been discontinued, and years of sun have changed the shade anyway. A workaround that usually works is to harvest weathered pieces from an elevation nobody looks at, move them to the spot that faces the street, and close up the donor wall with the nearest product still sold. For wood siding on older houses in Cordaville or Fayville, boards can be milled or sourced to match, primed on all faces and painted with the wall. Any disturbance of painted surfaces older than 1978 brings in EPA lead-safe rules, whatever the size of the patch.

Opening a damaged spot also lets you look behind the cladding. If the sheathing under a damaged spot is dark, soft or crumbling, water has been getting in, often from a window without flashing above it, a roof edge that ends against the wall without a kick-out, or a gutter that overflows. A brief on-site inspection should identify the source. Get the repair, the source of the water and any rot written up together, so you know whether the problem is truly local or part of a wider issue.

faq.q: The original siding color on my Southborough house is discontinued. What are my options?
faq.a: There are a few. The installer can relocate aged panels from a rear or side wall of your Southborough house to the damaged area, then put the newer stock out of sight. Another option is to re-side one full elevation, corner to corner, in the closest current color. For wood siding, repainting the repaired wall makes the match easy. Bring a sample panel when comparing options.

body: Full replacement on a Southborough house from the 1970s or early 1980s is mostly about fixing what the original builder left out. Many of those homes were wrapped poorly or not at all, windows were set with little more than caulk, and fiberboard sheathing has softened at corners and under sills. Pulling all the siding off is the only way to see and repair that.

With the wall open, a good crew replaces damaged sheathing, installs a continuous weather barrier with taped seams, and flashes every window and door, typically with a sill pan, side flashing and a head flashing lapped in the right order. This is also when rigid foam can be added over the sheathing to cut heat loss, provided window and door trim is built out to the new thickness. Asking for that option at the bid stage avoids surprises later.

Older houses add their own steps. In Cordaville or Fayville, a house may have original clapboard under one or two later layers, and removing them can expose sills and framing that have been wet for a long time. Paint from before 1978 is presumed lead-bearing, so EPA lead-safe containment and cleanup apply. Unknown older siding materials should be identified before removal. Whatever the age of the house, the estimate should explain how hidden damage will be found, priced and approved. Choose the new cladding last; vinyl, fiber cement, wood and cedar shingles all need the same sound wall beneath them.

faq.q: What hidden problems might show up when re-siding my Southborough house?
faq.a: On Southborough homes from the 1970s and 1980s, common finds include missing or torn house wrap, windows with no flashing, and soft fiberboard sheathing at corners and below windows. On older houses in Cordaville or Fayville, expect earlier siding layers, rot at sills and possibly lead paint. A good contractor will document what they find, explain the repair and agree on any added work before closing the wall.

body: The Sudbury Reservoir takes up about a tenth of Southborough, and wetlands and streams feed it from many directions. Lots that slope toward that water often have wet soil, and roof runoff dropped at the foundation adds to damp basements and frost heave at walkways. Getting downspout water well away from the house is the most important part of any gutter job here.

Long rooflines are typical of the town's late-twentieth-century colonials, so one eave can carry a very long gutter. Running it out of a roll-forming machine in the driveway gives a single continuous trough with no seams to drip. Size the gutter and downspouts to the roof area: a large roof draining into one corner can overwhelm a standard downspout in a summer storm, so a larger outlet or an extra downspout may be needed. Pitch every run toward its outlet and fasten hangers into solid fascia, checking for rot first.

Overhanging trees are the other constant. Oaks, maples and pines on wooded lots fill gutters quickly, and a clogged gutter overflows onto siding and trim, causing the rot that shows up later. Guards reduce cleaning, though no guard eliminates it; fine mesh handles pine needles better than coarse screens. Downspouts should discharge onto ground that slopes away, into an extension, or into buried pipe running to daylight. Icicles and frozen troughs in January usually trace back to heat escaping into the attic, which is a separate fix worth raising with the same contractor.

faq.q: My Southborough lot slopes toward wetlands. Where should my downspouts drain?
faq.a: Carry the water well away from the foundation, onto ground that slopes away from the house. On a Southborough lot that falls toward wetlands, downspouts can feed buried solid pipe that discharges downhill, where the water can spread and soak in. Avoid sending it toward a neighbor or directly into a wetland channel. If the yard stays saturated, a contractor can suggest a dispersal option suited to the soil.

body: Many Southborough houses from the 1980s and 1990s now carry their second roof or are due for one, and a few have a second layer laid over the first. The right way to replace those roofs is a full tear-off: it exposes the deck, so soft plywood can be replaced, and it gives a clean base for underlayment, eave membrane and new flashing.

These houses tend to have complicated roofs. Colonials with front gables, attached garages, dormers and bonus rooms create valleys and roof-to-wall joints that are the source of most leaks. Every wall intersection should get new step flashing, one piece per shingle course, with a kick-out at the bottom so water does not run behind the siding. Valleys should be lined with membrane and finished open or closed according to the shingle maker's instructions. Chimneys and skylights need new flashing kits rather than reused metal.

Winter in inland Worcester County means snow on the roof for weeks at a time, and ice dams form when heat escaping from the house melts that snow and the water refreezes at the eaves. Ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and valleys protects against leaks, but the cure is a cold roof deck: air sealing the attic floor, adequate insulation, and ventilation balanced between soffit intake and ridge exhaust. Bonus rooms with sloped ceilings deserve particular attention. On wooded lots, trimming branches back from the roof cuts down debris and moss. Ask roofers how they will handle each valley and wall joint, since those details decide how long the new roof lasts.

faq.q: Can a new roof go over the old one on my Southborough house?
faq.a: Sometimes it is allowed if only one layer exists, but it is rarely the best choice. Laying new shingles over old hides the deck, keeps worn flashing in place and adds weight. On a Southborough house from the 1980s or 1990s, a tear-off lets the roofer replace soft sheathing, install new eave and valley membrane and flash every wall joint correctly. If two layers are already there, a tear-off is required.

body: Roughly one Spencer dwelling in four sits in a building shared by two, three or four households, and only about 63 percent are lived in by their owners. That mix explains why vinyl is so common on the town's rental buildings. An owner looking after a two-family on a side street off Main Street rarely wants to stage the whole building for paint every several summers, and vinyl takes that chore off the list.

What goes on behind the panels matters more on these buildings than the brand. Many were framed in the late 1800s, when bootmaking pulled workers into the center, and the original clapboard under later layers often hides soft sills, rotted window heads and gaps where porches tie into the wall. Pull the old siding, open those spots, and make repairs before any wrap goes up. Then tape and flash each opening, starting at the sill and finishing with a head piece that overlaps the sides. Because about 68 percent of Spencer homes predate 1980, that tear-off almost always disturbs lead paint, so the crew must follow EPA RRP practices: ground cover, a closed-off zone and a verified cleanup, with extra care around entries tenants use every day.

At about 925 feet, Spencer sees colder nights and heavier snow than towns in the valleys to the east, and vinyl shrinks noticeably in the cold. Panels have to be hung loose enough to slide, with room left at each end so a January morning does not pull them out of their channels. On a tall multi-family wall, a thicker panel resists wind buckling, and staging should be planned so the building stays usable. Tenants deserve written notice of the dates and of which entrances will be blocked.

faq.q: What should tenants in my Spencer two-family expect when the building gets new vinyl?
faq.a: Some noise, blocked entrances for a few days, and a crew working outside their windows. Because the building is almost certainly older than 1978, the old siding comes off under lead-safe rules, which means plastic on the ground, windows kept closed near the work and a careful daily cleanup. Give tenants the schedule in writing, tell them which doors will be affected and when, and ask them to move cars, grills and furniture away from the walls before work starts.

body: The Spencer Town Center Historic District began in 1986 as a strip of Main Street between High and North Streets and later grew to take in the worker housing along Grove, High, Mechanic, Pleasant and Wall Streets. Many of the houses there went up when boot factories were drawing families into the center in the later 1800s, and they were sided in painted wood lap. With nearly three in ten local homes older than 1940, a lot of that original wood is still on the walls, some of it hiding under later coverings.

Assess old boards before condemning them. Clapboard tends to fail first along the bottom courses, under sills and where porch roofs meet the wall; the upper stories often hold up well. Where most of a wall is sound, replacing only the failed runs, matched to the existing reveal and butt thickness, keeps the house consistent with its neighbors. Corner boards and casings on mid-century revival and late Victorian houses set the frame the clapboard fills, so new boards should meet them at the same depth. Fiber-cement lap can stand in for wood where owners want longer paint cycles, provided the reveal and trim match.

New wood clapboard should be primed on every face and cut end before it is nailed, and set over a thin drainage gap so it dries from behind. Use ring-shank stainless nails, which hold in old sheathing and will not stain. On houses this old, lead paint is a given, so scraping, sanding or pulling boards follows EPA lead-safe rules. The district is on the National Register, which by itself does not limit an owner's choices, but owners on those streets may want to check with the town before changing a facade.

faq.q: Is it worth saving the original clapboard on my house on Pleasant Street in Spencer?
faq.a: Often it is. Old-growth wood in original clapboard is denser than most new stock, and boards that have survived this long are usually sound wherever paint has protected them. A contractor can probe each wall, replace failed runs with matching boards and prepare the rest for paint. The work must follow lead-safe practices because of the paint's age. Full replacement makes more sense only if rot is widespread or the boards are badly split across most of the wall.

body: For a Spencer owner with a century-old two- or three-family, fiber cement offers the painted-clapboard look these buildings were built with, a much longer interval between paint jobs, and a material that will not burn. That last point appeals to many owners of multi-unit buildings, especially where houses stand close together in the older streets around the center.

Old framing needs checking first. Fiber cement weighs far more than vinyl, and a building from the late 1800s may have board sheathing, walls that lean or bow, and studs softened where water got in years ago. Sound out the sheathing, sister or replace damaged framing, and fur out walls that are noticeably out of plumb so the courses run straight. A crooked wall that looks fine under vinyl will show every wave under a rigid plank.

Cutting creates silica dust, and on an occupied building that is more than a nuisance. A careful crew cuts mostly with shears or a saw hooked to a vacuum, keeps the cutting table away from windows and tenant entries, and cleans up daily. Detailing follows the manufacturer's instructions: a flashing piece behind each butt joint, sealed cut ends, clearance above every porch roof and above the ground, and trim sized to the building. At Spencer's elevation, with snow that piles against walls each winter, the bottom clearance matters more than most owners expect, because plank ends sitting in packed snow will wick water. Ask whether the price assumes factory-finished planks or primed boards for field painting, since that changes how often the building needs paint.

faq.q: Is fiber cement a good fit for an older multi-family building in Spencer?
faq.a: It often is. It looks like painted wood, holds paint far longer and does not burn, which many owners of multi-unit buildings appreciate. The cautions are weight, which means the old framing should be checked and walls straightened first, and dust control during cutting while tenants are home. Detailing at porch roofs and the ground line also matters in Spencer's snowy winters. Done carefully, it gives a long-lived, low-maintenance exterior on a building that will stay in service for decades.

body: Late Victorian is one of the two styles listed for the Spencer Town Center Historic District, and houses of that kind often mix siding types, with clapboard below and shingles in the gables, on upper stories or around bay windows. Some of those shingles are plain; others are cut in fishscale, diamond, or wavy patterns. When a house on High or Grove Street has lost a section of its decorative shingling, new cedar cut to the same shapes can put it back.

Matching starts with a careful record. Count the courses in each band, measure exposure, trace the butt shapes, and photograph the transitions where the shingles meet clapboard or trim. Specialty cuts are available in standard shapes, and unusual ones can be made to order. Each shingle needs two corrosion-resistant nails, positioned so the course above hides them, and the wall behind should let the shingles dry, with a breathable wrap and a ventilation mat or thin furring. Cedar laid tight against a damp wall cups and splits early.

Snow and cold shape the details at about 925 feet. Bottom courses should sit high enough that drifts and plowed snow do not bury them, and roof-to-wall joints need sound flashing so meltwater does not run behind the shingles. Decide on finish early: most Victorian shingle work was painted or stained, often in colors that contrast with the clapboard below, and pre-primed or pre-stained shingles coated on all sides hold paint best. Reaching a gable three stories up over a tight side yard takes proper staging. Any older shingles being removed probably carry lead paint, so removal follows lead-safe rules.

faq.q: The patterned shingles in the gable of my Spencer Victorian are falling off. Can they be matched?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Common shapes like fishscale and diamond are still made in cedar, and a shop can cut unusual patterns to order from a sample. A contractor should remove a sound shingle to measure its width, thickness and butt shape, then rebuild the damaged section course by course. Check the cause too: missing flashing at the rake or a gutter overflow above is often why the gable failed, and new shingles will not last until that is fixed.

body: Spencer's center grew fast in the late 1800s, and the houses from that boom carry most of their character in their trim. Bracketed eaves, porch posts and railings, window heads with small cornices and wide corner boards were made in the shops of the era, and many of those shapes are not sold as stock lumber today. When they rot, the right repair is a copy, milled in wood or cellular PVC from a sample or a tracing of the original.

Look first where trim meets a flat surface. Water collects on top of window heads, on the upper edge of a water table, on porch floors at the base of columns and on the cap rail of a porch railing. Those are the joints where rot starts, so new pieces need a slope, a drip edge or a small cap flashing to send water outward rather than letting it sit. Bracket bottoms and the ends of fascia boards also soak up water through exposed end grain, and they should be sealed before painting.

Porches on Spencer's two- and three-family buildings deserve a careful inspection whenever trim is planned. Daily traffic, snow shoveled off the steps and water dripping from upper porches wear on post bases, railings and stair stringers, and loose railings are a safety issue for tenants, not just a cosmetic one. Cellular PVC works well for post bases, skirt boards and other low pieces that stay wet, provided the joints are glued and fastened to allow for movement. Since roughly 68 percent of homes in town predate 1980, scraping or removing painted trim must follow EPA lead-safe practices.

faq.q: Can the rotted brackets under the eaves of my Spencer house be copied?
faq.a: Yes. A woodworker can make new brackets from a surviving original, either by tracing the profile and cutting new ones from wood or by having them made in cellular PVC, which does not rot. If every bracket is damaged, the best-preserved one becomes the pattern. New brackets should be primed on all sides and installed with sealed end grain, and the eave above should be checked for leaks, since a dripping gutter or roof edge is the usual cause of rot.

body: Repairs in Spencer often start with figuring out what is actually on the wall. An older house in the center may have original clapboard on one side, asbestos-cement shingles added in mid-century on another, and vinyl patched on later. A falling limb, a cracked panel or one soft board beside a porch roof can usually be fixed without residing, but the repair has to match whatever material is on that particular wall.

Matching takes some legwork. Old clapboard comes in profiles and reveals that may need to be milled to order. Decorative shingles in a Victorian gable can be cut to match shapes still on the house. Discontinued vinyl colors can sometimes be found as salvage, or panels can be moved from a hidden wall to the damaged one, with new stock going into the hidden spot. Asbestos-cement shingles are no longer made; a damaged section can be patched with a fiber-cement shingle of similar size once the broken pieces are removed by the correct procedure.

On a rental building, speed matters. A hole in the siding lets water reach framing and the ceilings of units below, so a temporary cover the same day and a proper repair soon after protect both the building and the tenants. Find the cause while the wall is open: a porch roof without a kick-out, a gutter overflowing above, or a sill pitched toward the house. Because about 29 percent of Spencer homes date from before 1940, painted wood is almost always lead-painted, and disturbing more than a small patch calls for lead-safe methods.

faq.q: My Spencer house has asbestos shingles and one section is broken. What are my options?
faq.a: The broken pieces should be removed and handled under the rules for asbestos-containing material rather than simply pried off and thrown away. A contractor can then patch the area with fiber-cement shingles of similar size and texture, painted to blend. If many shingles are cracked, or you are planning other exterior work, it may make sense to have the whole layer properly removed and the house re-sided. Either way, avoid breaking, sanding or power-washing the old shingles.

body: Taking the skin off a Spencer house built during the wire and boot years is a little like an excavation. The first clapboard is often still nailed to the boards, with a later jacket of cement-asbestos shingle over it and, on top, aluminum or vinyl from a more recent owner. Somebody needs to identify each stratum before the pry bars come out, since the asbestos-bearing shingle has to be taken down and hauled away under its own set of rules, apart from the general demolition.

With the walls bare, the building tells you what it needs. Plank sheathing on framing well over a century old may be punky at the sills and corners, and many window openings were never flashed at all. Carpentry comes first. After that, a wrap lapped like shingles, pans under every sill, tape up the jambs and across the heads, and a diverter at each spot where a porch roof butts the wall. Owners hoping for warmer apartments can add an insulating board layer now, provided jambs and casings are built out to the new depth. Roughly two-thirds of local housing predates 1980, so lead paint is all but certain, and the EPA renovation rule governs how the old material comes off and how the site is cleaned.

Tenants are often part of the picture. About a quarter of Spencer's homes share a building with one to three other units, and on those jobs the sequence matters: which elevation is opened first, how porches and stairs stay safe, where the dumpster sits and how many days each side remains exposed. Ask each bidder for a written order of work, a separate allowance for framing repairs, and a plan for protecting porches, parked cars and the house next door.

faq.q: There are several old layers on my Spencer house. Should the new siding go over them?
faq.a: Not on a full replacement. Removing everything down to the boards is what exposes decay, gives the new wrap and flashing a proper surface, and keeps the wall from growing so thick that window trim no longer fits. If any layer is cement-asbestos shingle, that one has to be removed by the proper procedure before the rest of the work moves ahead. Some framing repair is normal once the walls are bare, and a separate line for it in each bid makes the quotes easier to compare.

body: Spencer sits at about 925 feet, high enough that winters bring more snow and ice than in lower-lying towns to the east. Gutters here have to carry not only rain but the weight of packed snow and ice along the eaves, and a system that sags or pulls loose after one hard winter was usually hung too lightly. Hangers belong in rafter tails or solid fascia backed by framing, at close spacing, never only in trim boards.

Older multi-family buildings bring their own demands. A two- or three-family in the center can have a large main roof plus porch roofs on two or three levels, each needing drainage. Wide gutters and oversized downspouts handle big roof areas better, and upper downspouts should be piped down past lower porch roofs rather than spilling onto them, where water wears out shingles and ices the steps tenants use. Gutters should be pitched toward their outlets evenly and installed so the back edge sits under the drip edge.

In the older parts of town, houses stand close, and runoff needs to be planned with the neighbors in mind. Downspouts should not empty toward an adjacent foundation or across a shared driveway, where water can freeze into a sheet of ice. Extensions, splash blocks or underground pipe can carry water to a safe spot. On sloped lots, outlets on the uphill side should be piped around the house. A gutter estimate should show where every downspout will go and how far its water will travel.

faq.q: Why do the gutters on my Spencer house pull away from the roof every winter?
faq.a: Usually because they are not anchored firmly enough for the snow and ice load at Spencer's elevation. Gutters fastened only to trim, or with hangers spaced too far apart, sag under ice and eventually tear loose. Rehanging them with closely spaced hidden hangers screwed into the rafter tails fixes most cases. If ice builds up heavily at the eaves, the attic should also be checked for poor ventilation or heat loss that melts snow on the roof.

body: Spencer has a lot of old framing under its roofs. Nearly three in ten homes were built before 1940, and many of those are two- and three-family buildings and Victorians in and around the town center. Over the decades their roofs have often been covered more than once, and the framing beneath may include sagging ridges, undersized rafters or boards softened by long-ago leaks. A roof replacement is the time to find out.

Strip everything to the deck. With the old layers gone, the crew can check plank sheathing, replace or overlay damaged sections with plywood, and see whether rafters need sistering before new shingles add weight. At about 925 feet, snow loads and ice dams are real concerns, so self-adhering ice barrier should run from the eave edge well up the roof, in every valley and around chimneys. Many older houses here were built with no attic ventilation at all, and adding soffit intake with a ridge vent, along with sealing the attic floor, is what keeps the roof cold enough to stop ice dams forming.

Steep Victorian roofs and tall multi-family buildings make safety and logistics part of the project. A proper crew uses roof jacks, harnesses and anchors on steep pitches and plans debris chutes or dumpsters so nothing lands on a neighbor's car or a tenant's porch. Chimneys, dormers and porch-roof tie-ins are where most leaks begin, so their flashing should be new. Ask each roofer how they will handle rotten decking, whether ventilation is included, and how they will coordinate with tenants. Architectural shingles over a sound, vented deck should last twenty-five years or more.

faq.q: The ceiling of the top-floor unit in my Spencer three-family stains every winter. Is it the roof?
faq.a: Possibly, but in Spencer's winters the usual culprit is an ice dam rather than a worn-out shingle. Heat from the top unit escapes into an unvented attic, melts snow on the roof, and the water refreezes at the cold eaves and backs up under the shingles. A roofer should check both the roof surface and the attic. The fix often combines ice barrier at the eaves, added ventilation and air sealing, along with any shingle or flashing repairs.

body: Sterling's housing divides almost exactly at 1980, the Census median, and the newer half is where most vinyl work happens. Subdivision houses from the 1980s onward were often sided in builder-grade panels or in wood that has been repainted a few times, and both are reaching the age where owners start comparing replacement options. With more than four in five homes standing alone on their own lots, these are usually straightforward single-family jobs.

Height above sea level shapes the details. The town sits around 500 feet up, in the shadow of Wachusett Mountain, and houses on open fields or hilltop lots take wind that a sheltered valley lot never sees. Thin panels loosen and chatter there. A heavier gauge, a starter strip nailed tight to a level line, and fasteners at the closer spacing the manufacturer calls for in high-wind zones keep the bottom courses from unzipping in a gale. Leave the nail heads slightly proud so each panel can still slide as it heats and cools.

Before any of that, the old siding should come off so the wall can be read. On houses of this generation, the weak spots are usually the sheathing under window sills, the band where a deck ledger was lagged through the siding, and any corner where a gutter has been overflowing. Fix soft sheathing, lap the housewrap shingle-style, and tape every window flange before the first panel.
