Start the first course a hand's width above the planting beds, and hold each shingle with a pair of stainless nails driven where the next row will cover them.

Inside Westford Center, Forge Village or Graniteville, find out what a house originally wore before trading clapboard for shingles. Shingling a house that was always clapboard changes how it looks from Main Street or Prescott Street, and although the National Register status of those villages does not by itself prevent it, the change can look wrong. Where shingles are original, match the exposure and the coursing pattern. With stain refreshed every several years, or factory-stained shingles from the start, a shingled wall here should last two to four decades.

faq.q: The cedar shingles on the shady side of my Westford house are turning green. What can I do?
faq.a: Green and black growth means the wall stays wet too long. Prune back branches to let in sun and air, keep sprinklers off the wall, and pull mulch away from the lowest course. A gentle wash with an oxygen-bleach solution and a garden-hose rinse removes most growth; avoid pressure washing, which shreds the wood. When the shingles are eventually replaced, a drainage gap behind them and a breathable stain containing mildewcide will keep the problem from returning.

body: In Westford Center, near the old Common, the Colonial, Federal and Greek Revival houses get much of their dignity from carpentry at the edges: pilasters at the corners, a deep band of frieze below the eaves, molded cornices and framed doorways. The Italianate town hall of 1871 shows a later, fancier taste. When rot reaches any of that work, the right repair reproduces the shape, milling a matching piece or scarfing new wood into sound old wood, rather than nailing on a plain board that sits flat and wrong.

On the town's newer houses, the trim is plainer, and the trouble spots repeat from house to house. Sills built nearly level hold rain and decay from the front edge inward. Garage door casings sit in plowed snow and puddles. The skirt board behind a deck ledger stays soaked when the ledger went on without flashing. Fascia and rakes soften behind gutters that spill over. Pushing a screwdriver into each of those areas before planning a siding project reveals how much is really sound.

Low, wet locations call for cellular PVC. Rot cannot touch it, it holds paint, and it cuts and routs like wood, but it grows in summer heat, so joints are bonded with PVC cement and pinned with stainless trim screws. Wood is still the better material where a molded profile has to match an old village house. Above every window and door, a formed cap flashing slipped under the housewrap should send water over the face of the new casing instead of behind it. Ask each bidder plainly whether rotten pieces will be removed or just covered with bent aluminum.

faq.q: Rot has started at the base of the casing beside my Westford garage door. What is the fix?
faq.a: Cut out the decayed lower portion and splice in cellular PVC, which does not mind sitting in slush and splash. The siding beside it rarely needs to come off. Then deal with whatever caused the rot: no cap flashing over the door, a gutter that overflows at that corner, or a driveway pitched toward the opening. If those stay as they are, the new piece will face the same water, even if PVC survives it better than wood did.

body: In Westford, siding repair calls tend to sound alike. A limb from the woods behind the house punches through a wall in a nor'easter; a gust lifts a row of vinyl near a gable peak; one downspout has been spraying the same corner for years; a deck put up without proper flashing has been feeding water into the wall beneath it. If the remainder of the house is in good shape, fixing the damaged area alone is the right call.

Finding a match takes effort. Vinyl that has weathered since the 1980s no longer looks like a new carton of the same color, and many profiles from that decade have been discontinued. Options include the nearest current panel, or a swap: pull original pieces from an elevation nobody sees, such as behind a deck or a shed, use them on the damaged front, and side the hidden spot with new stock. On the wood houses of Forge Village, Graniteville and Westford Center, individual clapboards can be removed and replaced with milled boards of the same profile, back-primed and painted along with the wall around them.

Rotten siding is a symptom, and replacing it alone treats only that. Water running down a roof-to-wall joint that lacks a diverter soaks the wall right below it. A seam leaking in a gutter overhead softens whatever sits beneath. An unflashed ledger rots the band joist and the boards around it. Any repair proposal should say what let the water in and include stopping it. On village houses older than 1978, opening up more than a small patch of painted wood brings in EPA lead-safe work rules.

faq.q: A storm brought a branch down on my Westford siding. Can the damaged part be repaired by itself?
faq.a: Usually it can. Panels, clapboards or shingles can be swapped piece by piece, provided matching material can be found or milled. Have the contractor look behind the damage as well, since an impact can tear housewrap or crack sheathing that nobody sees from outside. With a big limb, check the gutters and roof edge too. Storm damage is often covered by homeowners insurance, so photograph everything before cleanup starts.

body: Half of Westford's homes were built after 1983, the Census median, and a great many of them still have the siding the builder chose. Forty-odd years in, the cladding, the trim and the hidden flashing behind them usually give out together: paint failing on every elevation, punky spots just above the foundation, brown streaks under window corners. At that point, re-siding the whole house solves the problems in one coordinated job instead of a string of patches.

On houses from that period, most of the value is in fixing what the old siding concealed. Builders then often left housewrap ripped or unfinished, set windows with minimal flashing, and let the lowest strip of sheathing take years of splash. Peeling the house down to bare sheathing allows every damaged sheet to be swapped, a full wrap to be lapped from the bottom up, and each window to be flashed in sequence, pan first and head last. Owners wanting a warmer house can add foam board outside the sheathing at this point, so long as casings and jamb extensions are deepened to suit the thicker wall.

The villages need a different plan. In Forge Village and Graniteville, the bulk of the housing went up in the second half of the nineteenth century, and opening a wall there can expose first-generation clapboard beneath one or more newer coverings, sometimes asbestos-cement shingle that has to be removed under its own rules. Sound original wood on the street side may be worth saving, and lead paint should be assumed, so EPA RRP methods govern the removal. For any house in town, ask bidders how hidden framing damage will be handled and priced, how they will protect plantings, and which wrap and flashing products are specified.

faq.q: What problems usually turn up once the old siding is off a 1980s Westford house?
faq.a: The usual list is torn or incomplete housewrap, windows set without tape or sill pans, and soft, stained sheathing below window corners and along the bottom of each wall. Deck ledgers bolted straight to the sheathing with no flashing are another frequent find. A trustworthy contractor will walk you around the open walls, show you each issue, and price the repairs before any new siding is hung.

body: Westford is a wooded town, and trees set the terms for gutters on many lots. Broad leaves pile up every autumn, conifers shed needles in every season, and when the trough clogs, the overflow lands on exactly the parts of the house that suffer most: fascia, siding and the basement wall. Choose a guard for the specific trees on the property. A stainless micro-mesh stops needles; a hooded cover lets broad leaves slide past.

Roof shape comes next. The larger houses built in town during the 1980s and 1990s often have a main roof, a garage roof, dormers and several valleys, and a valley can pour a summer cloudburst into one short stretch of gutter. Where that happens, a second outlet or a three-by-four downspout keeps the gutter from spilling over at the inside corner. A six-inch profile, formed in one length per eave, handles the long runs, and hidden hangers screwed into framing at close spacing carry the snow and ice that pile up through a Westford winter.

Then plan the discharge. Every downspout should release water well out from the foundation, by long extensions or by solid underground pipe that daylights downhill, and that matters most on houses with finished basements, where a damp foundation wall turns into ruined carpet and drywall. Near Nabnasset Lake and Forge Pond, where some lots tilt toward the water, outlets should spread water across planted ground rather than shoot a single stream down the slope. Ask for a simple drawing that marks each downspout and where its water ends up.

faq.q: My Westford basement is finished. Where should the downspouts send their water?
faq.a: As far from the foundation as the lot allows. Use extensions several feet long, or connect each downspout to buried solid pipe that empties at a low point in the yard or into a drywell. Check that the ground pitches away from the house all the way around. The downspouts below valleys and inside corners carry the heaviest flow, so give those priority. If the basement still feels damp after storms, have the grading and the foundation looked at.

body: At roughly 407 feet, Westford holds its snow, and a roof can stay white from one storm to the next for much of the winter. That makes ice dams the most common roofing complaint in town. Heat escaping from the rooms below warms the sheathing, the snow on top melts, the water trickles down to the cold overhang and freezes there, and the next melt backs up beneath the shingles. Curing that begins inside the attic, with open soffit intakes, an exhaust vent at the ridge, and every leak from the living space sealed, so the roof stays as cold as the air outside. A self-sealing membrane along the eaves and down each valley is the backup.

Many Westford houses from the 1980s and 1990s have busy roofs, with dormers, valleys and second-story walls rising from first-floor roofs. Every one of those joints is a place for water to get in. Each sidewall should get new step flashing finished with a diverter at its lowest end, and every valley needs a proper lining, whether open metal or woven shingle. Most of these roofs are on their first or second covering, so stripping to the deck lets the crew re-fasten loose sheathing and replace soft spots.

Village houses need a different approach. In Westford Center, Forge Village and Graniteville, the deck may still be the original boards, sometimes laid with gaps for wood shingles, and new plywood over them gives asphalt a flat, solid base. Chimneys on those houses typically need new step and counter flashing cut into the mortar joints. Ask each roofer about their ventilation plan, how decking repairs will be priced, and how they will protect gardens during tear-off. A properly vented architectural shingle roof should last a quarter century or longer.

faq.q: Why do ice dams form on only one side of my Westford roof?
faq.a: Usually that side either gets less sun or sits above a warmer attic. Bath fans exhausting into the attic, recessed ceiling lights, a loose attic hatch or a cathedral ceiling with no vent channel can all heat one section of the deck. North-facing slopes also hold snow longer. Sealing those leaks, adding insulation and improving ventilation in that area deal with the cause, and a membrane along the eaves protects against leaks while the fix is underway.

body: Vinyl is a minority choice in Weston, and it is worth being honest about where it fits. On a street of painted wood colonials and estate-era houses, plastic lap can look out of step. It earns a place on detached garages, pool houses, barns and some of the plainer postwar houses put up after Route 128 and the Turnpike opened the town to subdivision, especially where the owner simply wants an exterior that never needs a brush.

When it is used, the product and the trim make or break it. Choose a premium, thicker panel with a narrow, wood-like reveal and a matte surface rather than a glossy one, and pair it with real-width casings and corner boards in PVC or wood instead of the slim plastic accessories that come in the box. Color matters on a block where neighbors are painted wood; muted whites, grays and historic tones blend in better than bright stock colors. Every panel still needs room to expand, with nails centered in the slots and left a hair loose.

The wall underneath deserves the same attention as on any older house. About 65 percent of Weston's homes predate 1980, and with a median year of 1964, most postwar houses still have some original painted wood under whatever is on them now. Removing it means EPA lead-safe work, with sheeting, containment and a careful daily cleanup. A house that falls within the local historic district should have any switch of material cleared with the town before ordering. Installed this carefully, vinyl serves roughly twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Will vinyl siding on my Weston garage clash with the wood-sided house?
faq.a: It can be made to blend in. Pick a panel whose exposure matches the clapboard on the house, use a matte, low-sheen finish, and match the color to the house paint as closely as possible. Trim is the giveaway, so use corner boards, casings and fascia of the same widths as on the main house, in painted PVC or wood. From the street, a garage done this way usually reads as part of the same property.

body: Weston's older houses were nearly all painted lap siding, and the town has unusually many of them. About 23 percent of its homes predate 1940. Along Route 20, the Boston Post Road Historic District stretches roughly three and a half miles past the Golden Ball Tavern and Josiah Smith's tavern from the 1760s and 1750s. Up North Avenue, Kendal Green takes in the Whitney Tavern, houses built by the Hobbs tanners and houses the Hook and Hastings organ works built for the people in its shop.

On those buildings, the boards are part of the architecture. Before ordering, measure exposure and board thickness on each elevation, since back ells and later wings may not match the front. Corner boards, water tables, window casings and cornices set the proportions; new clapboard has to end against them at the same depth so the shadow lines stay crisp. Vertical-grain cedar or pine holds paint much longer than flat-sawn stock. Prime every face and end before installation, and nail with stainless or hot-dipped fasteners so rust does not bleed through the finish.

Shade is the other Weston factor. With more than 2,000 acres of forest, wetland and fields and so many lots under mature trees, north walls can stay damp for days, and clapboard nailed tight to the sheathing cups and peels. A drainage mat or thin furring behind the boards lets the back side dry. Removing old painted siding on pre-1978 houses falls under EPA lead-safe rules. If the house sits within the town's local historic district, find out what review applies before switching away from wood. Repainted on a steady cycle, new cedar lap siding has a service life on the order of twenty-five to forty years.

faq.q: Why does paint keep peeling from the clapboard on my Weston house?
faq.a: Peeling usually comes from moisture getting behind the paint. On shaded Weston lots, walls stay damp, and boards nailed directly over sheathing cannot dry from the back. Leaks at window heads, gutters and roof edges add water too, and interior humidity can push through walls without a vapor control layer. Fixing the source, then re-siding over a drainage gap or at least back-priming new boards, gives paint a much better chance. Lead-safe practices apply when scraping pre-1978 paint.

body: Fiber cement draws Weston owners who want painted clapboard without the scraping cycle, and it can be a good fit for the plainer postwar houses, for the much larger homes now going up in their place, and for additions where real wood would be hard to keep up. It holds paint, will not rot, is not attractive to insects or woodpeckers and stands up well in the damp shade of wooded lots. With almost nine in ten homes owner-occupied, most buyers are thinking in decades, and the product is rated for thirty to fifty years.

The look depends on choosing proportions that suit the house. A narrow reveal and a smooth finish usually read better on Colonial-style houses than the wide, wood-grained profiles common on builder homes. Corner boards, casings and frieze boards should be wide enough to hold their own against the siding. On a large house, long walls and tall gables mean the boards are heavy and awkward to handle; plan staging so they can be installed safely and without cracking.

Installation details matter. The boards need clearance from grade, roofs and decks, with flashing at every butt joint and a kick-out wherever a roof meets a wall. Cut ends should be sealed with the manufacturer's recommended primer or paint. Cutting releases crystalline silica, so ask how dust will be controlled. For a property inside Weston's local historic district, ask the town before trading wood for a cement board; National Register listing alone does not dictate the choice.

faq.q: Can fiber cement look right on an older house in Weston?
faq.a: On a plain wall far from the street, it often can. Choose a smooth board with a narrow exposure that matches the original clapboard, and keep the existing trim or reproduce it at full depth. Avoid embossed wood-grain finishes, which look out of place on older houses. On the street facade of a house in one of the historic districts, original or matching wood is usually a better choice, and the town should be consulted first.

body: Shingled walls look at home in Weston. Parks, fields, wetland and forest cover more than 2,000 acres of the town, and 37 roads carry scenic designation, so many houses, barns and sheds sit among stone walls and mature trees where weathered cedar blends in. Wealthy families began building country places here from the 1860s, and where one of those estate-era houses still has its original shingle work, such as patterned courses, flared skirts or curved walls, it is a key part of the design.

Copy that work instead of simplifying it. Record the exposure and the coursing, photograph any fancy-butt or staggered rows, and measure the angle of each flare before the old shingles come off. Under tall trees a wall can stay damp most of the day, and cedar fastened flat against the sheathing cups, splits and grows moss. A ventilated mesh or thin battens behind the courses give the back side room to dry. Two stainless or hot-dipped nails per shingle avoid streaks, and the lowest course should finish well clear of beds and soil.

Decide the finish before ordering. Raw white cedar goes gray, but the sunny side of a Weston house silvers in a season or two while shaded walls stay brown or mottled with mildew, and the effect can last years. Semi-transparent stain or factory-finished shingles even out the color at the cost of periodic recoating, and paint, suited to some formal houses, asks the most upkeep of all. Pre-1978 painted shingles must come down under EPA lead-safe rules. With air behind them and sound fasteners, the new courses should last twenty to forty years.

faq.q: My Weston house has flared shingles at the bottom of each story. Can that be reproduced?
faq.a: Yes. Flares are built by adding a tapered strip or kick at the base of each story so the bottom courses curve outward. A skilled crew can replicate the original flare by measuring the angle and projection before removing the old shingles. The detail takes extra time, but it is an important part of the house's character, and simplifying it changes the look noticeably. Photograph and measure everything before work starts.

body: The face of a Georgian or Federal house in Weston is mostly its woodwork. Cornices, pilastered doorways with pediments, corner boards and capped window casings set the proportions, and the same holds for the houses that went up after the 1860s as country estates and for the older buildings along the Post Road and in Kendal Green. When those parts decay, the new pieces have to match the old profiles; a flat board from the lumberyard dropped into a molded cornice is obvious from the sidewalk.

Rot gathers in predictable spots: sills, the lower ends of corner boards and door casings, porch posts and column bases, and the top of a cornice wherever a gutter spills. Test each with an awl, because fresh paint can hide mush. If the original piece is mostly sound, cut back to good wood and let in a new section with a glued scarf joint instead of replacing the full length. Mahogany, Spanish cedar and other rot-resistant woods, or cellular PVC for plain parts in wet spots, reduce return visits. Coat every joint and all end grain before the finish paint.

Lead is close to a certainty on this woodwork. About 65 percent of Weston homes were built before 1980, so scraping, sanding or pulling trim almost always triggers EPA lead-safe rules, and the written plan should spell out containment and cleanup. If the house is in the town's local historic district, ask about review before changing materials on visible trim. Repair the source of the water as well, whether a missing drip cap, a failed gutter or a splash zone at grade, or the new work will not outlast the old.

faq.q: Can the rotted door surround on my Weston Federal house be saved?
faq.a: Often a good part of it can. A carpenter can remove only the decayed sections of pilasters, plinths or the pediment and splice in new wood milled to the same profile. The bottoms of pilasters and the top of the pediment usually suffer most, since that is where water sits. Prime all new pieces and sealed joints before painting. If the surround is too far gone, it can be copied in full from measurements of the original.

body: A house with a few bad boards on an otherwise healthy wall rarely needs full replacement. In Weston, that might be a run of clapboard rotted beneath a leaking window on an early house along North Avenue, a split shingle course on an estate-era home, or a section of 1960s siding damaged by a falling limb on a wooded lot off one of the scenic roads. Patching keeps original material and costs far less than re-siding.

The repair depends on two things: stopping the water and matching the wall. Find out why the boards rotted, whether from a sill without a drip edge, a gutter end that overflows, a missing kick-out flashing or a bush holding moisture against the siding, and fix it before new boards go in. Then match exposure, thickness and profile; older clapboard may need to be milled to match. New boards should be primed on all sides and the paint feathered into the surrounding wall so the patch disappears.

Weston's tall trees and shaded lots add their own problems, including mildew, woodpecker holes and branches scraping walls. On houses built before 1978, repairs that disturb painted wood beyond a small area fall under EPA lead-safe rules. An on-site assessment should confirm whether the damage is isolated or part of a broader moisture problem, and a good contractor will tell you honestly if the wall needs more than a patch.

faq.q: Woodpeckers keep damaging the siding on my Weston house. What can be done?
faq.a: Woodpeckers are common on wooded lots and usually drum on cedar or wood siding while looking for insects or making noise. Repair the holes promptly with matching material so they do not attract more pecking, and check for insect activity in the wall. Deterrents such as reflective tape or netting can help in the short term. Fiber cement is a long-term option for walls that are hit repeatedly, though it changes the look.

body: Weston's housing runs from eighteenth-century taverns and farmhouses on the old roads to the postwar houses that followed Route 128 and the Turnpike, and a complete re-side turns up different trouble in each. The oldest walls may have plank sheathing, no insulation and repairs layered from several eras. Houses from the 1950s through the 1970s, the core of a stock whose median year is 1964, tend to show soft sheathing under windows, at outside corners and behind decks.

Everything comes off down to the sheathing, and then the crew reads the wall. Replace rotted boards and any framing that has gone soft, wrap the house in a continuous weather barrier lapped from the bottom up, and pan and tape each window and door before new cladding goes on. Many owners add a layer of rigid foam at this point, which means building out the casings so the trim still sits proud of the siding. On houses older than 1978, lead-safe handling applies from the first pry bar to the final cleanup.

Big houses need a schedule that protects them. Working one elevation at a time keeps any wall from sitting open in a rainstorm, and a good crew watches the forecast before stripping. Since nearly all of Weston's homes are single detached houses, the decisions usually rest with one owner, which makes the written scope the most important document: it should say how hidden rot will be priced, which products are proposed and how trim on the visible facades will be kept or reproduced. If the property is in the local historic district, ask the town before changing materials.

faq.q: Should I add insulation when re-siding my 1960s Weston house?
faq.a: It is usually worth it. Houses from the 1960s often have thin wall insulation, and rigid foam over the sheathing reduces heat loss through the framing. The extra thickness means window and door trim must be extended, and the siding must meet the roof and foundation cleanly. Ask the contractor how those transitions will be handled and whether the added foam affects warranties for the siding or windows.

body: Tree debris is the main gutter problem on Weston houses. More than 2,000 acres of the town are forest, fields and wetland, and countless lots sit under a full canopy, so troughs fill with leaves every fall and with needles, catkins and twigs the rest of the year. Once they clog, water spills over the front, soaks the fascia, runs down the siding and collects at the foundation.

Match the guard to what grows overhead: micro-mesh where conifers drop needles, a sturdier perforated cover where broadleaf trees dominate. Oversized downspouts clog less often. On the large new houses with complicated roofs, valleys pour concentrated water onto particular corners, and those runs need bigger troughs and extra outlets. Seamless aluminum formed on site avoids leaky seams, and concealed hangers driven into solid framing carry winter snow and ice without sagging. Lead every downspout well away from the foundation, particularly near wetlands where the soil already holds water.

Some older houses do not have hung gutters at all. A number of estate-era homes and houses in the historic districts have built-in wooden gutters set into the cornice, sometimes called Yankee gutters. They are part of the architecture, and they can usually be rebuilt where the wood is rotted and relined with a membrane, copper or another metal, sloped properly to the outlets. Tearing them out for hung aluminum changes the cornice line and can create new leaks where the roof meets the wall.

faq.q: Should the built-in wooden gutters on my Weston house be swapped for aluminum?
faq.a: Usually not. Built-in gutters are part of the cornice, and removing them changes how the house looks and can create new problems where the roof meets the wall. In most cases they can be repaired by replacing rotted wood and relining them with a modern membrane, copper or another metal. The relining should be properly sloped to the outlets. A well-relined built-in gutter can last for decades.

body: Roofing in Weston covers two very different kinds of houses. Many postwar homes from the 1950s and 1960s are being replaced by much larger houses, and those new roofs bring many valleys, dormers, chimneys and skylights, each a flashing detail that needs care. Older homes in the historic districts have simpler forms but older decks and masonry chimneys, and their roof color and texture matter to the streetscape.

Whatever the house, peel-and-stick membrane belongs along the eaves, through each valley and around every chimney and skylight. Step flashing at walls and dormers should be replaced, not reused, with kick-out flashing at the bottom of each roof-to-wall joint. Chimneys need sound counterflashing. Attic ventilation should be checked, since many older houses have little, and balanced soffit and ridge venting helps keep the roof deck cold and limit ice dams.

Trees are a constant factor on Weston's wooded lots. Overhanging branches drop debris that holds moisture and fills valleys, scrape shingles in wind, and can fall during storms. Cutting them back before a reroof protects the new roof. On older houses, choose a shingle color and texture that suits the house and its neighbors; some owners in the historic districts consider wood or slate-look products. Installed with that care, an architectural asphalt roof in Weston should hold up for somewhere between a quarter century and fifty years.

faq.q: What roofing works best on a historic house in Weston?
faq.a: It depends on the house and what was there originally. Houses of that age may originally have had wood shingles or slate, and some owners choose those again. Architectural asphalt shingles in muted colors are a practical option that suits most houses. Copper or lead-coated flashing suits older chimneys and valleys. If the house is in the local historic district, check with the town before choosing a material, since roofing can be subject to review.

body: Weymouth's head count jumped from 32,690 to 54,610 over two postwar decades, and the modest one- and two-story homes thrown up for those newcomers still dominate most blocks. Those houses, with a median build year near 1964, are where vinyl usually goes. Many already wear a first generation of it, thin and faded, or aluminum that has dented and chalked, and owners are ready for something that will not need paint.

Salt and wind change the spec near the water. On the North Weymouth shore and along Hingham Bay, gusts get under loose panels and peel them off a wall, so specify a thick panel whose nailing edge is doubled over for strength, a starter strip fastened at close spacing, and corner posts nailed solidly top to bottom. Stainless or coated fasteners last longer in salt air than bare steel. Inland, near Whitman's Pond or South Weymouth, a standard-weight panel hung loosely in its slots is usually enough. Wherever the house sits, strip the existing layer so someone actually sees the sheathing and the window flashing; about 71 percent of the town's housing went up before 1980, and pre-1978 paint underneath triggers RRP lead-safe removal.

East Weymouth needs a different conversation. Its Queen Anne, Shingle-style and Colonial Revival houses depend on patterned shingles, brackets and deep trim, and covering all of that with vinyl can erase what made them worth restoring, which is why restorations such as those under way on Hillcrest Road keep those details. On those houses, decide before ordering which parts stay exposed or get copied in wood or PVC, and keep vinyl to the plainer walls if it is used at all.

faq.q: My North Weymouth house faces Hingham Bay. Can vinyl survive that wind?
faq.a: Yes, when both the panel and the nailing are picked with gusts in mind. Choose a product carrying a high wind-load rating and a stiffened, doubled hem, and hold the crew to the tighter fastener interval the maker publishes for exposed lots. Pay special attention to the bottom starter and the outside corners, since wind usually lifts siding from the bottom or the edges. Stainless or coated nails resist salt corrosion better than plain steel.

body: Weymouth has some of the oldest clapboard in the region. A house on Sea Street dates from about 1650, and the Front Street Historic District beside Weymouth Landing holds close to 150 buildings and sites on 77 acres, many of them 18th-century capes and Georgian houses, including one at 160 Front Street from about 1720. A former shoemaker's shop at 99 Front Street, now a home, is a reminder that the town's shoe trade ran from the early 1700s until Stetson closed in 1973.

On houses that old, the siding is evidence of how they were built. Before removing anything, measure the reveal and thickness on each wall, look for hand-planed boards or beaded edges, and note how the clapboard meets corner boards, window frames and the sill. Early houses often have tighter exposure on the front than on the back or an ell. Where boards are sound, keep them and replace only the failed ones with matching stock milled to the profile. The district is a historic listing; ask the town whether any local review applies before changing materials.

Salt air and wind-driven rain off the harbor and the Fore and Back rivers shorten paint life on wood. Prime new boards on all faces and seal cut ends before installation, set them over a narrow drainage gap so the back face can dry, and fasten with stainless nails, which will not rust or stain the paint. With about 22 percent of Weymouth houses built before 1940, much of this work involves paint far older than 1978, so containment and cleanup under the EPA RRP rule are part of every job.

faq.q: Can damaged clapboards on my 18th-century Weymouth house be replaced without losing its character?
faq.a: Yes, if the work is selective. Keep every sound original board, and replace only the ones that are split or rotted, using new stock milled to match the old profile, thickness and exposure. Fit the new boards into the existing pattern rather than redoing whole walls. Prime them on all sides and paint them with the rest of the elevation. Because the house is old, assume lead paint and plan for RRP containment.

body: Salt is the reason many Weymouth owners end up looking at fiber cement. Painted pine or cedar on a house facing Hingham Bay, or perched along the Fore River or Back River, gets sandblasted by wind and soaked by spray, and the paint lets go years sooner than on the same house built near Whitman's Pond. Cement-based planks do not rot or soften, and a coat applied in the factory outlasts brushed-on paint by a wide margin. For the postwar capes and colonials that make up most of town, they also give back the painted-board look vinyl only approximates.

Hardware is where coastal jobs differ. Ask for stainless or heavy hot-dip galvanized nails, rated by the maker for salt exposure, and for the tighter nailing schedule the instructions call for in high-wind zones. A plank's sawn end pulls in moisture like a wick, and near the harbor that moisture carries salt, so every end cut on site gets primer before it goes up and every board-to-board joint gets a flashing tab behind it. Hold the planks clear of soil, decks, steps and any roof surface, and where a wall rises out of a roof, finish the step flashing with a diverter that kicks water away from the wall. On low ground, given how exposed Weymouth is to rising water, a generous clearance at the bottom course is cheap insurance.

On East Weymouth's Colonial Revival and Queen Anne houses, fiber cement can replace failing clapboard walls, but corner boards, casings and frieze boards need to be as wide and thick as the originals or the facade looks shrunken. Dry cutting throws silica, which on North Weymouth's tightly packed cottage streets means a vacuum-shrouded saw or shears and a cutting spot away from the neighbor's windows.

faq.q: Does fiber cement hold up better than wood on a North Weymouth waterfront cottage?
faq.a: In most cases it does. It will not rot, insects ignore it, and a factory finish holds up to salt air for many more seasons than paint on wood. The installation still decides the outcome: salt-rated fasteners, primed cut ends, flashed joints and clearance above grade and decks. Weight is seldom a problem on a small cottage, but ask how the crew will stage and cut on a narrow lot.

body: The shingled houses of Weymouth are concentrated in East Weymouth, where Queen Anne and Shingle-style homes, plus a number of Colonial Revival houses, wear cedar across whole walls, on upper stories or in their gables. Many carry fishscale, diamond or sawtooth bands. A repair on one of those houses has to reproduce the band, its exposure and where it starts and stops; a gable reshingled in plain straight courses looks wrong from across the street.

Shore houses put cedar through a harder test. Wind off Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor drives salt into the grain, and untreated shingles there turn silver within a few seasons, faster on the windward side than the lee. Plenty of North Weymouth cottage owners want exactly that weathered look, but they should expect the walls to age at different speeds. Fasteners matter more on the coast than anywhere: only stainless steel survives salt air without rusting, bleeding dark streaks and losing grip. Behind the courses, a crinkled drainage wrap or ventilated mat lets the wall dry out between nor'easters, which can add years to the shingles.

Away from the water the threat flips from salt to shade. Lots near Whitman's Pond and the woods of Great Esker Park keep walls cool and damp, and shingles there grow mildew unless branches are thinned and the cedar is treated or stained. For an even color anywhere in town, shingles dipped in stain at the factory, coated front, back and edges, age more uniformly than those stained after installation. On an older house where the shingles were painted, removal falls under EPA lead-safe rules, so ask how the crew will contain the debris.

faq.q: How do I match the patterned shingles on my East Weymouth Queen Anne?
faq.a: Identify each pattern and its exposure first, whether fishscale, diamond, octagon or another cut. Many shapes are still made, and a carpenter can hand-cut unusual ones from a template traced off an original. Replace whole bands rather than single shingles so the design stays continuous. Stain the new shingles before or right after installation so they blend while the colors settle.

body: Weymouth's trim divides along its timeline. East Weymouth's Victorians are dressed in brackets, turned porch posts, spindle rails and deep cornices, and owners restoring those houses usually want every salvageable piece kept and the rest copied faithfully. The 18th-century capes and Georgian houses along Front Street and Summer Street are plainer, with modest cornices and flat casings, and their repairs should stay just as plain rather than borrow profiles from a modern catalog.

Salt shortens the life of anything wooden near the shore. Window sills, the feet of corner boards and porch post bases catch wind-driven rain and spray first, and on houses along the bay or the Fore and Back rivers they are usually where decay starts. Press a pick into those spots before any siding contract is signed. Sound original wood can be patched with epoxy, primed and painted; failed pieces can be copied in primed wood or in cellular PVC, which handles coastal wet well at sills and post bases provided long runs are fastened to allow for seasonal growth.

The postwar houses that make up most of Weymouth have simpler needs: fascia boards behind leaking gutters, rake boards at the gable ends and the frames around garage doors. Replace rotted pieces before new siding goes on, never after, so moisture is not sealed behind fresh cladding. About 71 percent of Weymouth homes were built before 1980, so most of this trim carries old paint, and scraping, cutting or pulling pre-1978 trim calls for RRP containment and a documented cleanup.

faq.q: Can the original porch brackets on my East Weymouth Victorian be saved?
faq.a: Frequently they can. Brackets with soft spots can be dug out, filled with epoxy consolidant and repainted. Ones too far gone can be duplicated in wood or cellular PVC, using a sound original as the pattern. Before rehanging them, check the porch roof and gutter above for leaks, which is usually what rotted them. Handle old painted brackets with lead-safe practices.

body: In Weymouth, repair work tracks the weather and the distance to the water. On the North Weymouth shore and along the rivers, nor'easters tear vinyl loose, split old wood boards and drive rain into gaps around windows and outside corners. Farther inland, near South Weymouth or Whitman's Pond, the calls are more often about rotted bottom courses on wood siding, vinyl cracked by a mower or snowblower, or a wall stained by a gutter that has overflowed for several winters.

Repair the reason, not just the boards. Wind damage on a shore house frequently starts at an under-nailed starter strip or corner post, and rehanging the siding with heavier fastening keeps the next storm from repeating the job. Decay near the ground points to soil, mulch or downspouts emptying against the wall; on low-lying lots close to the water, puddling after storms may be part of it. Water stains spreading from window corners usually mean the flashing behind the siding has failed. Ask that the estimate explain the cause and price its correction.

Matching takes care on older houses. On an East Weymouth Victorian, patterned shingles and trim pieces should be copied closely enough that the repair disappears. Clapboard on the Front Street houses can be milled to the original profile and exposure. For faded or discontinued vinyl, a contractor may borrow panels from a hidden wall and patch that spot with the closest new color. Repairs that disturb pre-1978 paint call for RRP lead-safe practices. If the damage turns out to be widespread, price a full replacement for comparison.

faq.q: A storm tore vinyl off the side of my North Weymouth house. Can it be repaired?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Undamaged panels can sometimes be rehung, and cracked ones replaced. The key is working out why they came off, often an under-fastened starter strip or corner, and fixing that with fastening suited to a windy site. Check the housewrap and sheathing behind the damaged area for water before closing it up.

body: Most of Weymouth's housing went up during the postwar boom, and many of those houses are now on their second layer of siding, with original trim and window flashing that has worn out alongside it. When several walls show trouble, a full replacement usually makes more sense than repeated repairs, and it gives the crew a chance to see what is under the old cladding.

Removing everything down to the sheathing is where the value lies. On postwar houses, expect to find rotted sheathing below windows, missing flashing and gaps in old insulation. On North Weymouth cottages being redone, opening the walls may reveal framing that needs repair before anything new goes on, since a small house that has stood near the shore for decades often shows its age behind the siding. Install a continuous weather barrier, flash every window and door properly, and consider rigid insulation if trim can be extended. Pre-1978 paint calls for RRP containment during removal.

Material choice depends on location. Near the shore, fiber cement, high-wind-rated vinyl or cedar with stainless fasteners all handle salt and wind well. In the Front Street Historic District or on an East Weymouth Victorian, wood clapboard or shingles copied from the original keep the house's character; ask the town about any local review before changing materials there. A written estimate should list removal, new siding, trim and contingency carpentry as separate items so hidden damage is priced clearly.

faq.q: What should I expect when residing an older North Weymouth cottage?
faq.a: Expect some surprises once the walls are open. Cottages near the shore often have framing, sheathing or flashing that needs repair before new siding can go on. A good contractor will price contingency carpentry separately and show you what they find before proceeding. Choose materials and fasteners suited to salt air and wind, and plan for RRP lead-safe practices if the existing paint predates 1978.

body: Few towns in the region have as much water at their edges as Weymouth. Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor lie along the north, the Fore River and Back River reach into town, and Whitman's Pond sits inland. Weymouth is counted among the places most exposed to rising seas, and on low ground near the shore the water table is already close to the surface. Roof water dumped at the foundation only adds to it, so a gutter plan here is really a plan for getting water off the lot.

Start with metal that tolerates salt. Steel gutters rust quickly in coastal air, while seamless aluminum and copper hold up for decades. On houses facing the harbor, closely spaced hidden hangers fastened into the framing keep a run from flexing in wind or sagging under ice, and the back flange should tuck under the drip edge so gusts cannot drive rain behind it. Strap downspouts firmly to the wall so a storm does not peel them off, and use aluminum or stainless fasteners so dissimilar metals do not corrode where they touch.

Inland lots bring leaves instead of salt. Houses near Great Esker Park, Whitman's Pond and other wooded areas fill gutters every fall, and fine-mesh guards with oversized downspouts cut down on clogs and overflow. Postwar ranches and capes with long eaves benefit from a larger gutter profile in heavy rain. Wherever the house sits, run downspouts into solid pipe or long extensions that carry water well out from the foundation, especially on lots where the ground stays wet.

faq.q: What gutters last longest near the water in Weymouth?
faq.a: Seamless aluminum and copper both stand up to salt air, while steel rusts quickly near the shore. Aluminum is the usual choice for price and appearance; copper lasts longer and suits some older houses. Match fasteners and hangers to the gutter metal to avoid corrosion. Near the harbor, secure downspouts firmly and carry discharge well away from the foundation, since low-lying lots already hold water.

body: Wind decides how a Weymouth roof near the water should be nailed. Houses on the North Weymouth shore catch gusts straight off Boston Harbor and Hingham Bay, and a roof fastened to ordinary inland practice can shed tabs in its first serious storm. Request the high-wind fastening schedule printed in the shingle instructions, usually more nails per shingle, plus starter strips with sealant along both the eaves and the rakes, and drip edge nailed at tight spacing so the edge cannot lift.

Roof shapes vary by village. East Weymouth's Victorians stack towers, dormers and cross gables, and each joint where one plane meets another needs its own step or valley flashing, cut and lapped by hand. The 18th-century capes and Georgian houses around Front Street have simple gables but often a big center chimney whose flashing needs to be cut into the mortar and rebuilt. The postwar houses that make up most of Weymouth have plain gable or hip roofs, and since the typical one dates to about 1964, most have already been reshingled once or twice.

On any of these houses, stripping to bare boards lets the crew find soft decking and replace it before underlayment goes down. A peel-and-stick membrane at the lower edge and through each valley limits ice-dam leaks, while air drawn in under the overhang and let out up high keeps the attic close to outdoor temperature so snow melts evenly. Near the shore, choose flashing and nails rated for salt exposure, and ask whether the shingle warranty covers coastal wind speeds and what installation steps that coverage requires.

faq.q: How should a roof be installed to resist wind on the North Weymouth shore?
faq.a: Insist on the maker's coastal or high-wind method: six nails or more per shingle where specified, starter rows with sealant on both the eave and rake edges, and edge metal nailed close together. Pick shingles rated for high wind speeds and use nails and flashing that resist salt corrosion. Stripping the old roof also shows whether the boards underneath are solid enough to grip those nails.

body: Vinyl in Winchester is really two different conversations. On the houses that filled in after World War II, when the town grew from roughly 15,500 to 22,000 residents between 1950 and 1970, it is usually a sensible, low-maintenance replacement for tired wood or aluminum. Those capes, ranches and garrison colonials have plain walls and simple trim, and the town's median build year of about 1954 says there are a lot of them.

On the older streets the answer is more careful. Wedgemere and Firth–Glengarry are full of large houses from 1880 to 1920 with bays, wraparound porches, shingled gables and deep cornices. Putting vinyl on one of those means deciding, piece by piece, what happens at every transition: where panels stop below a shingled gable, how porch ceilings and columns are treated, whether window casings keep their depth. Badly handled, those joints are the first thing a passerby notices, and wrapping rich trim in coil stock erases the detail that makes the house worth looking at.

Whatever the age of the house, tear the old cladding off, check the sheathing, and flash every opening into a new housewrap before panels go up. Most Winchester houses predate 1978, so stripping painted wood requires EPA RRP lead-safe methods. Hang panels loose with clearance at the channels so they can move through hot and cold spells, and choose a heavier gauge for the long side walls of a colonial. Ask any bidder for a written plan covering corners, casings and how the siding will meet existing trim. Installed this way, vinyl serves twenty to forty years.

faq.q: Does vinyl make sense on a 1950s colonial in Winchester?
faq.a: For many owners it does. A postwar Winchester colonial usually has straightforward wall planes and modest trim, which vinyl covers cleanly, and it removes the repainting cycle that wood demands on shaded lots. The value depends on the installation: the old siding should come off, the sheathing and window flashing should be checked, and the trim plan should keep enough depth at corners and casings that the house does not look flat.

body: Colonial Revival is the style Winchester knows best, and it was built around painted clapboard. In the Wedgemere district, built up almost entirely between 1890 and 1920, and along Everett Avenue and Sheffield Road beside Upper Mystic Lake, the facades are composed of crisp board lines meeting wide corner boards, a defined frieze and molded cornices. Change the board width or crowd the trim and the house loses its balance.

Measure the existing exposure at the front and on the sides before ordering, and look at how boards finish at the corners, the water table and each window casing. Builders of that era frequently laid boards with less showing than today's standard lumber gives, so a custom run may be needed. With about 39 percent of Winchester homes built before 1940, plenty of houses here still have original wood under paint or under a later layer; open a section to see what remains and whether it can be repaired instead of replaced. Seal each new board front, back and ends, then set them over a ventilated gap of strapping or drainage mat so paint lasts.

Large houses need staged work. Strip and re-clad one wall at a time, closing each with barrier and flashing before the day ends, so the house is never left open overnight to a coastal storm. Paint applied before 1978 is assumed to contain lead, and disturbing it on these houses means EPA RRP containment, ground protection and cleanup. Ring-shank stainless nails will not rust or work loose, so the finish stays clean. Looked after with periodic repainting, new clapboard on a Winchester house gives a quarter century of service at the low end and as much as four decades.

faq.q: Can the clapboard on my Winchester Colonial Revival in Wedgemere be repaired instead of replaced?
faq.a: Often it can. Clapboard on Winchester's turn-of-the-century houses was typically high-quality wood, and individual split or rotted boards can be removed and replaced with matching profiles while the rest stays in place. Replacement makes more sense when large areas are soft or the paint has failed down to bare wood everywhere. A contractor should open a few spots to check the sheathing before recommending either approach.

body: Two quite different groups of Winchester houses are good candidates for fiber cement. On postwar homes, it offers the look of painted clapboard without the repaint schedule. On the larger Colonial Revival houses from the turn of the twentieth century, it can carry the same board lines as the originals while resisting the rot that eventually finds wood on shaded walls. Roughly 82 percent of local homes are lived in by the people who own them, and long-term owners are the ones who collect on a cladding that lasts thirty to fifty years.

Big, detailed houses make fiber cement a planning job. Every bay window, porch roof and cornice return is a place where boards must be cut, flashed and sealed, and the weight of each plank means a tall wall gets pipe staging or pump jacks, never just ladders. At each spot where a bay or porch roof dies into the siding, stop the planks a little above the shingles, tuck step flashing behind them, and finish the run with a diverter that sends water into the gutter. Back each end-to-end seam with a small flashing piece, and seal any edge the saw has touched.

Sawing the product puts crystalline silica in the air; insist on outdoor cutting with shears or a saw hooked to a vacuum, away from neighbors' open windows on Winchester's closer lots. Factory finishes come in a limited palette; on a street with strong historic character, choose a color and reveal that sit comfortably with neighboring houses, or use primed boards and paint on site. Houses on the hillside streets toward the Middlesex Fells may have tall downhill walls that need staging plans written into the bid.

faq.q: Can fiber cement match the look of the original clapboard on a Winchester Colonial Revival?
faq.a: Close enough for most owners, if the reveal and trim are chosen carefully. Fiber cement comes in smooth and wood-grain finishes and several exposure widths, so pick the one nearest the original boards. Keep corner boards and casings at their original depth. Factory colors are limited, so primed boards painted on site may suit Winchester houses where the color matters to the street.

body: Shingles are written all over Winchester's older neighborhoods. In Firth–Glengarry, the neighborhood between Wildwood Street and Wedge Pond that went up mainly from 1880 to 1900, architect Robert Coit used shingles generously, and Wedgemere's Shingle Style houses mix in with its Queen Anne and Colonial Revival homes. On these buildings, shingles shape the walls, flare over porches and curve around bays.

Replacing shingles on a house like that is restoration work. Measure the exposure, record the coursing, and note any patterned butts in the gables, whether scalloped, pointed or staggered, before stripping anything. Bends and flared courses may need shingles soaked or kerfed to follow the curve. These neighborhoods are National Register districts, and that listing by itself puts no limits on an owner, but it is still wise to ask the town whether any local review applies to your address before changing a shingled exterior.

Shade and water are the enemies. Mature trees, and lots near Wedge Pond, the Aberjona River and the Mystic Lakes, keep walls damp for long stretches. Lay a breathable spacer mesh under the courses so moisture behind them can escape, and choose a good penetrating stain, brushed on every face or factory-applied, to hold back mildew and graying. Fasten with stainless steel, a pair per shingle placed where the next row covers them, so iron stains never run down the wood. Hold the lowest row several inches clear of beds and lawn, and prune limbs that brush the wall. Cedar on a Winchester house treated this carefully commonly lasts two to four decades before the walls need reshingling.

faq.q: Is it possible to copy the decorative gable shingles on a Firth–Glengarry house in Winchester?
faq.a: Yes, with some preparation. Mills sell pre-cut fancy butts in the common shapes, and an odd shape can be traced and cut on a bandsaw from a sample. The installer should photograph and measure the existing gable work before removing anything, then reproduce the exposure and coursing exactly. Also check whether the town requires any review for exterior changes on your street before the work begins.

body: Winchester's older houses are trim-heavy. Wedgemere, Firth–Glengarry and the streets around Winchester Center are lined with porch columns, brackets, cornices, decorative gable boards and window surrounds, and William Firth's own gambrel-roofed house uses Doric columns. When those parts decay, the repair should reproduce them faithfully, in custom-milled wood or a PVC replica for spots that stay wet.

On a large house, start with a full trim survey before any work. Go around the whole building with an awl, testing the feet of porch columns, the undersides of rails, every sill, the bottom foot of each corner board, and the cornice wherever a gutter runs above it. Mark what is soft, what is cracked and what only needs paint. That list makes it easier to set priorities and often reveals a pattern: rot in one area usually traces to a gutter, downspout or flashing problem somewhere above it, and fixing that source matters as much as the carpentry.

On the Tudor Revival and stucco houses along Everett Avenue and Sheffield Road, trim joins stucco and brick, and those joints need flexible sealant and careful flashing so water does not get behind the stucco. On the postwar Winchester capes and colonials, the failures are simpler and more predictable: fascia behind overflowing gutters, rake boards that catch wind-driven rain, and flat sills that let water sit. Those parts can be replaced with cellular PVC or primed, sealed wood, and fixing them before any re-siding keeps rot from being trapped under new cladding. Since about 78 percent of homes predate 1980, nearly all trim work here disturbs lead paint, and EPA RRP rules govern containment, scraping and cleanup.

faq.q: What is the best material for replacing porch columns on a Winchester Victorian?
faq.a: It depends on where the column stands and how it is detailed. Painted wood is easiest to match for turned or fluted columns, and a rot-resistant species with sealed end grain lasts well if the base is kept dry. Composite or PVC columns resist rot and suit spots that stay damp. Whatever the material, add a vented base or plinth so the column does not sit in water on the porch floor.

body: On a large older Winchester house, a full re-side is rarely needed to fix a problem. More often the damage is local: a few split clapboards on the weather side, shingles lifted by a storm, rot confined to a corner board or the area under one window. Targeted repair keeps the original material in place and avoids disturbing walls that are still performing.

Matching is the hard part. Turn-of-the-century clapboard can have a narrower exposure or thicker butt than today's stock, and shingle coursing may vary from wall to wall. Measure several spots before ordering, and if the profile is unusual, have it milled. Where a few original pieces are needed for a front repair, they can sometimes come from a less visible wall, with new material installed there instead. On postwar houses with vinyl or aluminum, faded color is the usual challenge.

Every repair should end with the cause fixed. Rot under a window often points to a failed sill or missing head flashing. Damage along the lowest courses may trace to a clogged gutter spilling from above, or to soil and mulch heaped against the wall. Downspouts that dump right at the corner of the house are another common source, and a short extension often solves it. Houses on lower ground near Wedge Pond and the Mystic Lakes, or under heavy tree cover, dry slowly and show these problems sooner. On houses from before 1978, which covers most of Winchester, disturbing painted surfaces beyond small areas brings in EPA lead-safe practices.

faq.q: How do I find matching clapboard for a repair on my older Winchester home?
faq.a: Start by removing a damaged board and measuring its thickness, width and exposure. A lumberyard or millwork shop can run boards to that profile if stock sizes do not match. Prime the new boards on every side, install them with the same nail pattern as the originals, and paint the whole wall section so the repair blends in. If the paint predates 1978, follow lead-safe practices when removing boards.

body: A median build year around 1954 and about 78 percent of homes built before 1980 put many Winchester houses past due for new siding. Re-siding everything at once is worth it when the damage is spread around the house: soft trim on several sides, cracked or loose cladding on more than one wall, and repairs that keep coming back. Small multi-family buildings make up just 8 percent or so of local housing, so a single family is nearly always the one choosing.

Most of the benefit comes during the stage when the walls are bare. Stripped of old layers, the house shows its true sheathing, decayed boards get swapped out, a seamless weather barrier wraps the frame, and each window and door is given new pans and taped flanges. On older houses, empty wall cavities can be insulated before new siding goes on. Older layers may need testing for asbestos, especially gray cement shingles common in the mid-twentieth century, and painted wood on any home older than 1978 comes off under the EPA RRP program, with containment and cleanup.

On Winchester's large turn-of-the-century houses, the architectural details need a plan before the old siding comes off. Cornices, window surrounds, porch connections and shingled gables should either be preserved in place or reproduced, not buried under new cladding or simplified to plain boards. Take the house one elevation at a time so no wall stays exposed when weather turns. A good bid in Winchester lists, as separate lines, tear-off, hazardous-material testing and abatement, allowances for concealed damage, the new cladding and the trim package.

faq.q: What should I watch for when re-siding a large older house in Winchester?
faq.a: Protect the details. Make sure the contractor plans how cornices, casings, porch trim and shingled gables will be kept or matched, since cheap replacements flatten the house. Ask how lead and possible asbestos will be dealt with, how many walls will be stripped at once, and what rate applies to rot discovered behind the old siding. Get references from similar houses and a clear written scope.

body: Winchester's landform sets the gutter plan. A central valley carries the Aberjona River south through Wedge Pond to the Mystic Lakes, and the eastern third of town climbs steeply into the Middlesex Fells. Houses near the water sit on low ground where soil stays wet, while houses on the slopes have to manage runoff that wants to race downhill toward a driveway, a foundation or the house next door.

Down near the ponds, distance is everything: carry each downspout's flow out past the foundation, by extension or underground line, and let it out where the yard drops away from the house. On hillside lots toward the Fells, route outlets so water spreads into lawn or planting areas instead of sheeting across a driveway, where it can freeze, or onto a neighbor's property. In both cases, size the gutters and downspouts to the roof area; complex roofs on large older houses concentrate water at valleys and inside corners.

Some turn-of-the-century Winchester houses still have built-in gutters, wood troughs set into the cornice and lined with metal. Those belong to the cornice design, and relining or patching them usually beats tearing them out for hung gutters that alter the roofline. On postwar houses and newer additions, seamless aluminum is the practical choice, hung on screwed brackets with the back edge under the drip edge. Where big oaks and maples arch over a roof, plan on guards plus a fall cleaning, and probe the fascia boards before any new trough is mounted on them.

faq.q: Are the built-in gutters on an old Winchester house worth keeping?
faq.a: Usually. Built-in gutters are wooden channels formed into the eave and sheathed with metal, and they are part of the cornice design on many turn-of-the-century houses. Leaks usually come from a failed lining, which can be replaced with new copper or a membrane. If the wood around them has rotted, that needs repair first. Replacing them with hung gutters is possible but changes how the house looks.

body: The Queen Anne and Shingle Style houses of Wedgemere and Firth–Glengarry have some of the most complicated roofs in the area: intersecting gables, dormers, hips and many valleys. Each of those joints needs its own flashing, and a reroof on a house like that takes more planning, more staging and more time than a simple gable roof. A contractor should walk the roof, map every valley and wall joint, and explain how each will be flashed.

Postwar houses, with a median build year in town of about 1954, are simpler but often have older decking or more than one layer of shingles. Take them down to bare boards, renew the bad ones, and put self-sealing membrane at the eave edge, running it past the warm wall line, and down each valley. Step flashing should be replaced at every wall and dormer, and chimneys counter-flashed into mortar joints. Air entering at clear soffits and leaving through a ridge vent, with the ceiling below sealed tight, keeps snow from melting unevenly and refreezing at the edge.

Two other things matter in Winchester. Steep lots toward the Fells make roof access, staging and debris removal harder, so ask how the crew will handle them. And the town took part in a rooftop solar pilot in 2011; if you are considering panels, plan the new roof and the solar layout together so you do not need to remove panels for a reroof soon after. Laminated asphalt shingles nailed exactly as the manufacturer specifies should be good for a quarter century or more on a Winchester roof.

faq.q: Should I reroof before adding solar panels on my Winchester house?
faq.a: If the roof is more than about halfway through its life, yes. Removing and reinstalling panels for a later reroof adds cost and disruption. Replacing the shingles first, with new flashing and underlayment, means the roof under the panels should last as long as the system. Ask the roofer and solar installer to coordinate mounting points and flashing so the new roof's warranty is not affected.

body: Route 128 opened in 1951, and over that decade Woburn grew by about 52 percent. The ranches, capes, split-levels and small colonials built for them still dominate many streets, and the city's median house dates to about 1968. A lot of those homes are now on their second cladding job, usually replacing either their original wood or an early vinyl or aluminum layer that has gone chalky, dented and loose at the seams.

The visible panel is the least interesting part of a Woburn vinyl job. The real decisions sit behind it. Will the old layer be stripped, or just covered? Stripping is almost always better, because it lets the crew look at the sheathing under every window and along the sill plate, swap rotten sections and put on a properly lapped wrap. Will insulating board go on? It improves comfort, but it thickens the wall, so every casing must be built out or the siding ends up flush with the window trim, which looks cheap and sheds water poorly.

About 63 percent of Woburn houses were standing by 1980, so the paint on old trim and clapboard is often lead-based, and stripping it brings in EPA lead-safe containment and cleanup. Close lot lines on postwar streets mean the neighbor's driveway and garden need protection too. When panels go up, nails should sit centered and slightly loose so vinyl can slide through hot and cold spells. In buildings with two to four units, about one in five Woburn homes, agree on one color and profile for the whole structure before ordering.

faq.q: Is it worth adding foam board under new vinyl on my 1960s Woburn ranch?
faq.a: For many owners it is. A ranch from that era usually has little insulation in the walls, and a layer of foam board under the vinyl cuts heat loss through the studs and gives the panels a flatter surface to lie on. The tradeoffs are a thicker wall, which means extending window and door trim, and careful flashing at each opening. Ask the contractor to show how the trim and flashing will be handled before you decide.

body: Fewer than one in five Woburn homes predates 1940, but the ones that do tend to sit in the old core around Woburn Center and along Main Street, where the 1790 House still stands. On those buildings, painted wood clapboard is the original cladding, and when it fails the right move is to replace it in kind, keeping the reveal and board thickness that set the look of the facade.

Measure before you buy. Write down the reveal on every elevation, and look at where the lap boards stop against the corners, the window casings and the skirt board at the foundation. Replacement stock has to land at the same depth, or the trim loses the shadow that makes it read. Some older Woburn houses carry hand-planed boards slightly off from anything sold today, which can mean a short custom run. Push an awl into the sills and the lowest few courses; rot there usually reaches well past what the paint shows.

Wood lap siding is also a fair choice on a 1960s Woburn colonial whose owner wants the real thing. Boards held off the wrap by a small rain-screen space keep their paint years longer than ones nailed tight against the wall. Choose fasteners that will not rust, seal the cut ends, and coat the backs and edges of every board before it is hung. Being this close to the coast, the city takes nor'easter rain sideways against its walls, so that air space and a metal cap over each window head earn their cost. Disturbing pre-1978 paint along the way brings EPA lead-safe work practices into play.

faq.q: Can I get clapboard that matches the old siding on my Woburn Center house?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. Pull one intact board from an out-of-the-way spot and carry it to a lumberyard. Plenty of profiles are still sold, and when one is not, a millwork shop can knife a batch to the same width, butt thickness and bead. Coat the new pieces on both faces and the edges, weave them into the courses already on the wall, and repaint that entire elevation so the new wood disappears.

body: Woburn's population climbed from about 20,500 to more than 37,000 between 1950 and 1970, and the houses built in that span are the main candidates for fiber cement today. Those homes have simple, broad wall planes that planks cover efficiently, and with a little over half of Woburn's homes owner-occupied, many families are looking for a cladding that will not need repainting every few years.

Start by checking the wall itself. Fiber cement is heavier than vinyl and much stiffer, so it shows every bow in the studs and every soft spot in the sheathing. Once the old cladding comes off, the crew should sight down each wall, shim or plane high and low spots, and replace damaged sheathing before the first plank is fastened. Planks need to be nailed into framing per the manufacturer's schedule. Prefinished boards reduce field painting, though every cut edge still needs a touch of primer or sealant.

Dust is a real issue on Woburn's postwar lots, where houses can stand close together and the neighbor's windows may be open. Cutting fiber cement releases crystalline silica, and the responsible approaches are shears, a dust-collecting saw, or wet cutting at a station set away from occupied spaces. Keep the bottom course clear of soil and paving, hold planks off the shingles where a garage or porch roof meets the wall, and back each joint between plank ends with a flashing piece. A good bid explains each of these steps.

faq.q: My Woburn split-level is close to the neighbors. How is fiber cement dust handled?
faq.a: Cutting fiber cement creates fine silica dust, so a careful crew uses shears where possible, a circular saw with a vacuum attachment, or wet cutting. The cutting station should be placed away from your neighbors' windows and doors, and the crew should clean up daily. Ask bidders to describe their dust control plan in writing. It protects the workers, your family and the people next door.

body: Cedar shows up on Woburn houses in two ways. A few of the city's nineteenth-century buildings were shingled from the start, and on those the job is copying the coursing that survives. Far more often, shingles are a deliberate break on a postwar house: the triangle of a gable over vinyl lap, the cheeks and face of a shed dormer, or the wall of a newer family room, giving a plain 1960s box some texture.

Plenty of Woburn yards run up against woodland, notably along Horn Pond Reservation and Forest Park. Under those canopies a shingled wall gets little sun, collects pollen and leaf grit, and can stay wet long after a storm passes. Cedar survives that only if its back side can breathe, which is the job of a crinkled drainage wrap or slim battens set between the housewrap and the courses. Hold the first course a good distance above soil, cut foundation plantings back so a breeze can reach the wall, and nail with stainless so no black streaks bleed down the face.

Settle the look before the first bundle is opened. Bare cedar goes gray on its own schedule, faster on the sunny side; bleaching oil pushes the whole house toward one even tone. Semi-transparent stain keeps a color for a few years at a time, and factory-coated shingles start out with every face protected. Shaded walls near the reservation benefit from a finish that includes a mildew inhibitor. Taking off old painted shingles from a pre-1978 wall means lead-safe procedures. Kept dry and well fastened, cedar on a Woburn house should give several decades of service.

faq.q: Will cedar shingles on a gable look right over vinyl on my Woburn colonial?
faq.a: They can look very good, if the joint between the two is done right. Where the vinyl stops, a trim board or band with metal flashing on top should kick water out before the shingles begin, so nothing runs behind the lower siding. Choose a stain color that complements the vinyl rather than tries to match it. Put a drainage wrap behind the cedar, fasten with stainless, and expect to recoat the stain every several years.

body: Trim on most Woburn houses is plain, the fascia, rake boards, window casings, door surrounds and garage jambs of a postwar ranch or colonial. Plain does not mean trouble-free. The spots that fail first are predictable: fascia behind a gutter that overflows, the lower ends of door casings at front and side entries, and garage trim that sits close to the driveway and takes splash, salt and snow from the plow.

Before any work, walk the house with an awl and push it into the bottom of each casing, the base of each corner board, and the fascia under each gutter run. Paint hides a lot, and soft wood behind a fresh coat is common. Small rotten sections can be cut out and replaced with a matching piece; long runs of fascia or rake that have gone soft along their length are better replaced whole. Cellular PVC handles the wettest spots well, though it moves with temperature, so joints should be glued and fasteners placed to allow for that.

Older buildings near Woburn Center are different. On a nineteenth-century front, cornices, window caps and door surrounds carry the period style, and replacements should copy the original profile rather than swap in a simplified stock board. Primed wood sealed on every face is usually the better match there. With about 63 percent of Woburn homes built before 1980, scraping or removing painted trim often falls under EPA lead-safe rules. Ask whether a bid replaces damaged trim or covers it with aluminum, since covering can trap moisture.

faq.q: The trim around my Woburn garage door keeps rotting. What is the best fix?
faq.a: Garage trim near the ground takes splash, snowmelt and road salt, so wood there wears out quickly. Replacing the lower jambs and casing with cellular PVC is a durable option, since it will not rot. Check what is sending water there, such as a gutter overflowing above the door, a missing drip cap, or snow piled against the jamb. Fixing those keeps the new trim lasting longer.

body: A lot of Woburn siding problems are local: a section of vinyl knocked loose in a windstorm, a few boards rotted around a single window, or panels cracked by a ball, a ladder or a snowblower. If the trouble stays in one area and the sheathing underneath is firm, fixing that area is cheaper and quicker than re-cladding the whole house, and nothing else gets disturbed.

Every repair should start by asking why the damage happened. Siding that is soft right under the eaves often points to a gutter leaking or spilling over. Rot around a window can trace to missing head flashing or a sill that pitches toward the house. Close-set postwar houses sometimes have downspouts that empty into the narrow space between buildings, where water splashes back onto both walls. A repair estimate worth having names the cause and describes how it will be corrected along with the boards or panels.

The second hurdle is making the fix invisible. Vinyl and aluminum hung decades ago have bleached in the sun, and many of those product lines were discontinued long ago, so a color off the shelf rarely lines up. A practical trick is a swap: harvest matching pieces from a wall nobody sees, install them at the front, and put the closest new product where it will stay out of view. Woburn has a lot of pre-1978 housing, and once a repair disturbs more than a small patch of old paint, EPA lead-safe procedures apply. In a two- to four-unit building, tell the co-owners before anyone starts cutting.

faq.q: Can a repair on my Woburn house match vinyl that is no longer made?
faq.a: It can usually get close. Bring a piece to a supplier and compare it with current profiles and colors, or relocate old panels from the rear of the house to the damaged front and patch the rear with new stock. If nothing is close enough, redoing one entire elevation from corner to corner tends to look cleaner than a mismatched rectangle. Ask to see the proposed material against your wall before agreeing.

body: With the median Woburn house built around 1968, many homes are wearing original or second-generation siding that has reached the end of its useful life. When panels are cracked on several walls, paint will not hold on wood, or water stains are showing around windows inside, a full replacement deals with all of it at once instead of patching the same problems year after year.

Mid-century houses often carry more than one layer. Under vinyl or aluminum there may be original wood clapboard or cement shingles, which can contain asbestos and should be tested before removal.
